subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
That this House urges the Government to immediately initiate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to lead off the debate today. As I am sure Hon. Members have noticed, the wording of the motion before the House today is taken from the PC Campaign Handbook for the 1984 election in which it is very clearly stated:
We advocate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power-
That is precisely what we will be debating today. It goes on further to state:
-and have opened the nuclear power approval process to the public.
I think that today's debate is really the debate of our times. It is something which involves the survival of all life. It really depends on our will to learn, to understand and to act on this issue if we are to survive the rest of the century.
On October 22 of last year my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), introduced a Private Members' Bill entitled the "Nuclear Power Act" which provides for three specific Acts to be taken by Parliament. The first is to invoke a moratorium on the new construction of nuclear facilities in Canada; the second is to hold a public inquiry; and the third is to hold a national referendum on the issue of nuclear power and nuclear energy in Canada.
Why have a full public inquiry? I think the Chernobyl accident has raised the concerns of many Canadians and made many of us realize why it is so important. I think that today it is important in the debate to hear what the alternatives are in terms of energy alternatives in the soft energy path. We should consider why we should be looking more carefully at the issue of safety and why we should be looking at the issue of mining and its affects on workers who have been involved throughout the whole of the nuclear cycle from cradle to grave. We should

May 15, 1986
Supply
consider the issues of transportation, storage, disposal, nuclear power itself, the movement of a lot of this material into nuclear weaponry and the effect of accidents.
I would like to begin my remarks this morning by dealing with the Chernobyl accident. I think it has raised the interest of many scientists and certainly of many people around the world.
When I first contacted the Department of National Health and Welfare and, in particular, the Atmospheric Environment Service, I was advised that because there are 28 atmospheric testing sites in Canada which had demonstrated an ability during the 1950s to give fairly accurate readings when atmospheric bomb testing was taking place in the Soviet Union, the United States or elsewhere, that, similarly, those 28 sites would provide accurate atmospheric and rainfall information throughout Canada. We found out that that, in fact, has not been the case.
In fact, just yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) rose in the House to indicate that new test sites will be opened in Terrace, Prince George and Revelstoke. Up until now the only information available from British Columbia, for the whole of British Columbia, has been from the tests taken in Vancouver. The majority of those tests were brought here to Ottawa to be tested, the information then being made available through the so-called hot line. As those who work on the hot line have pointed out, many of the staff members are left with the same basic information for two days. So if a person calls on two consecutive days they are getting essentially the same information. As I pointed out yesterday small communities in Alaska, such as Ketchikan, have had installed on-site equipment which can provide background readings, both atmospheric and rainfall, on a five-hour basis to be provided to the residents of Alaska.
Clearly, the proposal which was put forward by the Government on May 5 has not been adequate in terms of providing accurate information to Canadians. However, I must say that the information which has come to be available is not something about which Canadians should be overly alarmed, at least not enough to cause them to go out and drink iodine or take similar measures.
What we have to do is learn from what has happened in Chernobyl and take the type of intelligent steps which we should as a Parliament, particularly in light of the promise made by the Conservative Party prior to the last election. These promises were carried in headlines across the country in Toronto, Vancouver and elsewhere. They stated that one of the priorities of the new Government would be to call a full public inquiry into the nuclear industry, something which is very much needed.
As I learned under the administration of Mr. Trudeau from committees and in the House, it was impossible to obtain updated information. Every attempt taken by either the Conservatives or by the New Democrats to have an inquiry or to obtain accurate, updated information on what AECL and
AECB were really up to was blocked by the Liberals. I do not think many of us have forgotten the amounts of money which have historically been squandered in this area of concern, and the heavy water plants in Cape Breton are an example of that. Over $100 million of taxpayers' money went to keep those heavy water plants going while there was no use for that heavy water in Canada and no sale for it offshore.
The Conservatives seem to be changing ground rather quickly on the issue-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reponse to the campaign promise made by the Conservatives the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) wrote to one of my colleagues on June 4, 1985, and indicated the she did not intend to broaden her consultations beyond the industry and the provinces in relation to a full public inquiry into the nuclear industry. She went on to state:
-it is my view that a national inquiry on this topic is not a high priority at this time.
That is what the Minister of Energy had to say on behalf of a Government which clearly ran on a campaign promise to have a public inquiry into the nuclear industry.
It is also interesting to look to see what the present Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) had to say in a wire story which states:
Progressive Conservative MP Frank Oberle (Prince George-Peace River) said handling nuclear wastes from other countries could become a "lucrative business".
Now we can see why the Conservative Government is tending to shy away from the very important campaign promises which it made.
I would now like to quote from a 1982 issue of The Canadian Business Review. It is an excellent article written by Gordon Edwards, someone who long ago should have been given the Order of Canada for his work in relation to the nuclear industry. In his article he quotes from the draft of an internal Government review which states:
-it is doubtful "whether the nuclear industry will survive the 1980s".
The chart provided in The Canadian Business Review points out what the energy consumption by fuel type is in Canada. It

May 15, 1986
is well worth taking a look at these figures. Energy consumption directly from oil accounts for 52 per cent of our energy. With respect to natural gas, the figure is 23.5 per cent; coal is 3.9 per cent; and wood pulp 4.1 per cent. The total with respect to electricity is 16.5 per cent. Hydro is 11.4 per cent and coal-fired is 2.4 per cent. Nuclear power accounts for 1.3 per cent while oil-fired accounts for 0.7 per cent. Gas-fired accounts for 0.6 per cent and wood and others account for 0.1 per cent. Nationally, it is interesting to note how small is the amount of energy provided by nuclear power. Yet there are tens of billions of dollars which go into directly subsidizing this particular industry.
Under the section on energy in The Canadian Business Review article Mr. Edwards points out a number of key points, around which I think the debate should revolve, as to why there should be a full public inquiry. I refer to reactor safety studies. I think we must learn from Chernobyl and Three Mile Island that although many people for many years have told us that CANDU is the safest and best protected nuclear fission technology in the world, it is an area about which we need to study more closely. This should be done in a public inquiry where witnesses can be protected in giving evidence.
With regard to radioactive waste disposal, I recently had a chance to listen to Morris Udall, as did you, Mr. Speaker, who is now putting together what he himself describes as probably the largest, grandest scale project in the history of the United States. This project is the movement of nuclear waste from their sites to storage areas perhaps immediately below your own constituency, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

speechtext: That has been ruled out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
The issue of radioactive waste disposal is very important. It is a crucial issue in the United States. The Americans are trying to deal with it by the year 2000. We have no plans like that and there is certainly nothing before Parliament to deal in a parallel way with what is going on in the United States.
Regarding the issue of the highly radioactive wastes produced by the reactors, there exists in excess of 100 million tonnes of highly toxic low level radioactive waste called tailings. The amount of tailings at Elliot Lake alone would cover the Trans-Canada Highway three feet deep from Vancouver to Halifax. Those tailings are sitting there waiting for Canadians to come up with a way of dealing effectively with radioactive waste.
Regarding the decommissioning of nuclear facilities, there is a requirement to develop techniques and tools for the dismantling of the highly radioactive structures left at the end of the useful lifetime of a reactor. We know, for example, that Gentilly I is awaiting that kind of proper decommissioning. The argument about workers being thrown out of work if we were to have a moratorium on nuclear power and start decommissioning our nuclear industry simply does not stand
Supply
up under the scrutiny of economists and scientists who have looked at the amount of work required in the decommissioning of the existing sites. Similarly, specialized tools and skills would be needed to simply retube reactors during the period of a moratorium in order to keep the operations going as safely as possible.
Regarding energy self-sufficiency, Dr. Edwards made an important comment about evidence given by Sir Brian Flowers. He said the following:
Canadians should carefully weigh the advice of Sir Brian Flowers, a prominent British nuclear physicist, who warned in 1976 that "a major commitment to fission power and a plutonium economy should be postponed as long as possible." The reason for this is fundamental.
Plutonium appears to offer unique potential for threat and blackmail against society because of its great radiotoxicity and its fissile properties.
The construction of a crude nuclear weapon by an illicit group is credible. We are not convinced that the Government has fully appreciated the implications of this possibility.
That evidence was given in Great Britain before a royal commission. Many years ago, the Britons took this issue much more seriously than we do.
The Select Committee on Ontario Hydro Affairs took a look at the issue of accidents recently and had the following to say about the devastating and irreversible consequences of a major accident in a CANDU reactor:
It is not right to say that a catastrophic accident is impossible.
-The worst possible accident would involve the spread of radioactive poisons over large land areas, killing thousands immediately, killing others through increasing susceptibility to cancer, risking genetic defects that could affect future generations, and possibly contaminating large land areas for future habitation or cultivation.
Dr. Edwards goes on:
According to the Ontario Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning, the most realistic probability for a complete core meltdown in a CANDU reactor is about 1 in 10,000 per reactor per year.
It is interesting that that is precisely the same figure used by the Soviets in relation to Chernobyl, a state of the art graphite reactor built only a few years ago. The quote goes on:
With 23 reactors now committed in Canada, each expected to operate for 30 years or more, the over-all probability that a catastrophic meltdown will occur at one of these plants in the future is greater than 1 in 15-more than twice the probability of rolling a twelve with two dice-
Even non-catastrophic accidents can have a crippling impact. The cleanup following the Three Mile Island TMI accident in Pennsylvania is expected to take about ten years and cost $1 billion to $2 billion, but there is no assurance that cleanup efforts will be successful.
It is also interesting to look at the calculated probabilities for accidents in CANDU reactors. This information comes from the Atomic Energy Control Board itself as given to the Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning. The calculated probabilities for accidents are as follows: for loss of coolant, with one reactor it is one in 100 annually; with one reactor it is one in four over the reactor's lifetime; with 20 reactors, it is one in five annually, and with 20 reactors it is 99.7 per cent over their lifetimes. On core meltdown, something which has already occurred here in Canada, the probability is one in 10,000 for one reactor annually; one in 300 for one reactor's

May 15, 1986
Supply
lifetime; one in 500 for 20 reactors annually, and one in 15 for 20 reactors over their lifetimes.
The probability calculated by the Atomic Energy Commission itself is that one is as likely to roll a 12 with two dice as we are to have a meltdown at some point during the life of the reactors we have here in Canada. Again, that is a very important reason why there should be a full public inquiry into the issue of safety of existing complexes and wastes in Canada.
The only legislation for the protection of Canadians in and near nuclear sites, places like Toronto, is the Nuclear Liability Act passed by this House limiting off-site liability to a maximum of $75 million for each nuclear site. Comparable legislation in the United States, the Price-Anderson Act, an Act which is in the process of being amended, provides $560 million per site. It is now being suggested by the U.S. General Accounting Office that that liability should be increased far above $1 billion. That certainly appears to be a good example for us to follow. Financial institutions, not only in North America but in most of the world, are now reticent to finance nuclear reactors. As well, there are no insurance companies of which I am aware that are prepared to give liability insurance to any facilities in the world.
In British Columbia, the very excellent Bates Commission looked into the whole issue of uranium mining particularly but looked at the nuclear cycle as well. It had a number of interesting suggestions to make in relation to that. Regarding radioactive material in relation to Chernobyl and others, the U.S. geological survey had this to say:
High-level radioactive wastes produced by reactors are capable, in principle, of causing "millions to billions of fatal cancer doses... an admittedly unlikely scenario." The U.S. Geological Survey has pointed out that there isn't enough fresh water in the world to dissolve these wastes to "acceptable" levels of concentration.
That is something that concerns many Canadians right now, even though the addition of radioactivity from the Chernobyl accident is only one-twentieth of background levels. However, it is that amount that is added to already existing background levels that is of concern. This clearly raises the possibility of serious medical problems for people throughout Canada.
Dr. Edwards goes on:
The B.C. Medical Association considers it "irresponsible in the extreme for the Government of Canada to allow the further development of uranium mining and reactor construction until a safe, proven, permanent waste disposal technology is developed for the wastes that have already been produced."
If we as legislators do not listen to the evidence given by physicians before a Royal Commission on the effects of these kinds of contaminants on the general health and wellbeing of Canadians, to whom are we supposed to listen? Should we only listen to those who are promoting the technology? I think not, and I think for that very reason we should be moving vigorously and quickly toward the full public inquiry that was promised by the Government before the election.
The issue is very crucial. I know that my time is running out so let me end by reading what Dr. Edwards said about Dr. Bernard Feld:
Dr. Bernard Feld, Assistant Leader of the Critical Assembly Group in the World War II Atom Bomb Project, is one of many who have warned that the spread of nuclear technology will soon advance beyond the ability of human societies to control it:
Let me tell you about a nightmare I have. The mayor of Boston sends for me for an urgent consultation. He has received a note from a terrorist group, telling him that they have planted a nuclear bomb somewhere in central Boston. The mayor has confirmed that twenty pounds of plutonium is missing from Government stocks. He shows me the crude diagram and a set of the terrorists' outrageous demands ... I would have to advise surrender.
The issues surrounding the nuclear fuel cycle from cradle to grave are vast and important. I would like to end my remarks by talking about what I consider to be the other part of this issue that is rarely looked at by Parliament, parents, schools and physicians, and that is the effect of nuclear fear on young people in Canada and around the world.
According to a recent poll taken in British Columbia, 80 per cent of students fully expect to die a nuclear death and 80 per cent of them want to do something about it but do not know what to do. Clearly, during this period of time in the history of the world, one of the things this Government can do, in good faith since that is its policy, is hold a full public inquiry to investigate what is happening to uranium miners, nuclear wastes and the wastes being stored at CANDU facilities. That alone would fill a hockey rink waist deep with highly radioactive waste which is being improperly stored. Also, it should deal with the questions of radiation, its effect on individuals and its effect on the psyche of young people and people around the world.
Generally Canadians are not people who will get out and march, although in Vancouver close to 100,000 or more march year after year on the issue of nuclear energy. They demonstrate their desire for some kind of realistic investigation of it by the Parliament of Canada.
In my closing remarks I want to stress that it is important to understand the nuclear nightmares of young people, to understand the nuclear fear out there, and to act responsibly rather than irresponsibly and unresponsively to this very real issue, one of the most crucial issues of our time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like a clarification from the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). He seemed to mix two things today. He talked about nuclear war and tried to tie it in with the peaceful use of nuclear power in Canada. As he knows, there are no nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. In fact, we use nuclear power for peaceful purposes, such as the generation of hydroelectricity and isotopes which are used in the health field. If the NDP had its way, we would not have any of that expertise in Canada. By the way, we are a leader in that field.
Is the Hon. Member really being fair when he tries to tie in the peaceful use of nuclear energy with the phoney issue of it somehow being tied in with nuclear war?
May 15, 1986

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will deal first with the issue of nuclear medicine. As a matter of fact, the last time there was an opportunity to debate the issue in the House, 1 was unfortunately in hospital in Ottawa. Fortunately I had the opportunity for nuclear medicine to be of great assistance to me. It proved to be of great benefit. There is no one in my Party or in any Party who opposes the peaceful use of nuclear technology for medicine in particular. However, in tying the issues together, I think we have to understand that so far as we know the Chernobyl reactor was being used for peaceful purposes as well. It was being used to provide power to the City of Kiev and to the outlying area.
The issues before us are mixed. Approximately 85 per cent of the uranium mined in Canada is exported. A great deal of it goes to the enrichment plants in the big four-in France, Britain, the Soviet Union, and the United States-for enrichment to weapons grade material. The overwhelming majority of that is going into the 50,000 plus nuclear weapons which are constantly being upgraded around the world.
The Hon. Member said that there were no nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. That is a bit of a shell game. The Hon. Member knows full well that nuclear weapons are frequently tied up in downtown Vancouver, in Esquimau, in Halifax, and in various areas. The only difference is that there is a rope tying the boat to the dock. Often there are nuclear weapons in the downtown areas of many Canadian cities. That has never been denied by any Minister in the House or by anyone in the United States. In fact, those weapons are being brought in.
The reason there is a link between the issues is partly because of the Chernobyl incident. It is also because of the evidence which came forward from the Royal Commission in Great Britain. The expert evidence given by witnesses there such as Dr. Feld and others was that the real concern was that Governments were not scrutinizing as carefully as they should the highly radioactive plutonium waste which is sitting, for example, next to all our reactors in Canada. It is not being moved to be stored carefully and properly, perhaps in plutons or perhaps in other areas. I am sure we will have to develop a technology, a routing, and a system to get that waste to a proper long-term storage basin.
As those witnesses pointed out, there is linkage between peaceful sites or the peaceful utilization of nuclear material for electrical energy and for other uses and the no longer so remote possibility that terrorists will make use of plutonium and highly radioactive materials associated with peacefully used plants around the world. It is precisely for that reason we require a full public inquiry.
As the Speaker and myself learned at a meeting in the United States from Morris Udall, who is carrying this process forward for the U.S. Congress, probably the largest single industry between now and the turn of the century in the United States will be the decommissioning of reactors and the removal and safe containment of waste. It will be larger than the industries involved in the construction of highways and
Supply
buildings in the entire United States. It will be a massive industry.
For a variety of reasons our country is not looking at the possibility of terrorist activity. We are not looking at the need to deal with the hundreds of millions of tonnes of low-level radioactive waste or at dealing effectively with the whole concept of technology for decommissioning and proper longterm safe storage of the nuclear waste we already have at our nuclear sites.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I think the Hon. Member really does not have his facts together. He knows full well that probably one of the finest research projects is ongoing now in Canada on the safe storage of nuclear waste, and that the Americans, thank goodness, have contributed to and are participating in that research. We want to assure ourselves in Canada that not only do we have safe storage of nuclear waste but that they have the same technology and are storing it as safely as we are and in areas which are safe. I think the Hon. Member is being very unfair when he says that there is none of this going on. One of the most extensive research projects is going on in Whiteshell now on this very matter. Had he come to the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources to hear what was going on, as did his hon. friend behind him, maybe he would change what he just said. I wish he would correct the record.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the Hon. Member in my committee for years and years and years; "ta, ta, ta". This issue is a very important one. Government Members constantly want to slide away from the real issue. They ran an election on having a full public inquiry, and now they are thumbing their noses at the public of Canada and saying "ta, ta, ta".

I have looked at the budget, what is being spent in this country and in the United States on investigating technologies for safe and proper storage. It is piddling, compared with the taxpayers' money being spent to prop up a basically bankrupt industry. There are many other ways of providing energy safely over the long term in Canada, such as wind, tidal, peat, oil and gas. We have all kinds of alternatives which are far better. Even in Ontario there are far better alternatives than nuclear.
Because of the centralized control of a number of Financial institutions and certain vested interests, that Government over there is not prepared to live up to its campaign promise. That is the root of this debate. There are Canadians from coast to coast who want a full public inquiry into the safe and proper utilization of technologies for the storage of the waste, the decommissioning of those reactors, and dealing from cradle to grave with the whole issue of the nuclear cycle in Canada. That is what the debate is all about.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) is not aware of the large number of small and large contractors which are directly involved in creating and providing all the technology to keep these existing facilities going. Their concern, whether it is in relation to the tube reactor systems, the cement work or any of the work that has gone on at the site for construction and revamping, is about how Parliament is going to respond to the issue of decommissioning reactors and how Parliament is going to respond to the safe, proper storage and handling of uranium on its way to the sites and the wastes, to be stored properly over the long term.
I am saying that a full public inquiry is the way to go about providing assurances to those tens of thousands of workers in small and large corporations that are associated with the nuclear industry which, as the Member knows well, has been almost entirely funded by public dollars through Ontario Hydro, through AECL, or through our own public watchdog, the AECB.
I am talking about the need to provide accurate information to those small and large corporations associated with the industry so that the old red herring: "If we have a full public hearing and they talk about decommissioning, all you guys are going to be thrown out of work" will not be hurled. It is not true at all, as Morris Udall pointed out at our meeting in the United States. This is going to be an enormous project in the U.S. that will employ not just tens but hundreds of thousands of Americans in the process of decommissioning and the proper safe storage of nuclear waste in the United States.

-at Chalk River. This is unfortunate because the nuclear industry in Canada has played a vital role and will continue to play a vital role in providing electrical energy.

AECL designs reactors and supplies heavy water. It takes the lead in export marketing. Provincial utilities, like Ontario Hydro, New Brunswick Hydro, Quebec Hydro make the decisions on new capacity and undertake management of these facilities.
When the present facilities are completed and into production around the end of this decade, Ontario will have some 50 per cent of its hydro provided by nuclear energy. It will provide the base load of energy for the Province of Ontario for close to 10 million people by that time. Balanced against that 50 per cent, which will be provided by nuclear reactors located at Douglas Point in Bruce County, at Pickering and Darlington, another 50 per cent of the energy required will be provided by hydro.
These two forms of energy are compatible. They are probably less harmful to the atmosphere than oil fired or coal fired thermal generating stations. The base load is provided by nuclear energy; the peaking power by hydro. In Ontario that is especially important. We have vast supplies of hydro and uranium which fuel nuclear reactors.
Private sector industries throughout Ontario have provided the principle components for the CANDU reactor and they
May 15, 1986

perform the engineering services in Canada and abroad. In 1982 the Government undertook an extensive review of the whole nuclear industry. A 359 page report was issued called "Policy Review. Background Papers." There were 16 papers covering a range of reviews of public concern including questions of health, safety, environmental impact, waste management, reactor exports and non proliferation treaties.
In the nuclear industry as in the petroleum industry we have seen dramatic cut-backs in the amount of electricity needed, just as we have seen dramatic cut-backs in the amount of petroleum needed in the past eight or 10 years since the energy crisis. We have seen cut-backs in the number of nuclear reactors constructed.
At the Lennox generating plant, a massive 2,000 megawatt oil fired generating plant which has never produced any electricity for any sustained period of time was under construction in the early 1970s. It was completed in the mid-1970s. This oil fired electrical generating plant was designed to use bunker C or heavy residual oil which would have created enough electricity to provide half the needs of the City of Toronto. It was made obsolete because the price of oil went from $2 a barrel in 1971 or 1972 to $35 to $38 Canadian in the years 1979-80-81-82, which has dropped back to $13 or $14 U.S. I do not know what the cost of that plant was, but several billions of dollars were spent. It was made totally obsolete as a result of oil prices. We see Ontario moving to a supply of nuclear energy balanced by hydro electric energy.
My constituency has always been especially concerned about nuclear energy because Elliot Lake, a town of some 20,000 people, was developed and built around the nuclear industry. The plant at Elliot Lake produces vast quantities of uranium which is sold, not only to Ontario Hydro, and the United States in past years, but as well to Japan, France, the United Kingdom and West Germany.
That industry in Elliot Lake is facing fairly severe cut-backs over the next few years because the present contracts established in the mid-1970s will not all be needed. A couple of weeks ago we received word that a factory in Algoma will have to cut about 200 jobs during this calendar year. That is as a result of the restructuring of the contracts between Ontario Hydro and Rio Algoma mines. I hope that that cut-back can take place over a 12 or 18 month period so that the lay-off of 200 people at Stanley Mine can be accomplished through attrition with people taking early retirement or taking up new careers in order to avoid dramatic lay-offs, especially of young workers.	,
I call upon the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton), who is very concerned about these workers being laid off, to put a great deal of pressure on the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to change the UI regulations. If there is a generous program provided by Rio Algoma mines and Ontario Hydro, a lot of older workers would probably take early retirement. However, with the
Supply
present regulations they would have to sacrifice unemployment insurance benefits for a year. We just went through that in Sudbury where the youngest person in the labour force will probably end up being 45 years of age. If we had left the old provisions in place, allowing people to receive severance pay and early retirement benefits as regular income, older workers who are approaching 60 or 64 years of age would take early retirement, thus allowing younger workers in their 20s and 30s to retain their jobs.
Surely we need a more satisfactory method of making those large industrial adjustments. I cerainly hope that that provision of UI will be changed so that if Rio Algoma and Ontario Hydro come forward with a policy for retirement the benefits will not be treated as regular pay. They should not be. We are making adjustments for early retirement to facilitate industrial adjustments such as we are seeing in the nuclear industry.
People opposed to the nuclear industry will talk about the number of reactors which have been spun out over a longer period of time. That is happening in all energy industries. Although we do not like to see people laid off in any industry, we know that the conservation methods which Canada and other countries have implemented are in the best interest in the long term. We use so much petroleum and we know that resources of petroleum are finite and will eventually be used up.
Eldorado Resources, a uranium refinery in my constituency at Blind River, Ontario, is very active in the nuclear industry. It employs 180 people. It refines uranium from yellowcake to uranium dioxide which is then transported to Port Hope for upgrading to uranium hexafluoride. That industry is very, very dependant on the further upgrading policy of the Government of Canada which has been in place for many, many years. That is why I was very pleased by the Minister's comments which were carried in The Toronto Star on November 8, 1985. He indicated that the Government was going to toughen its policy. Elliot Lake, Ontario, and northern Saskatchewan are the two principal uranium mining areas in Canada and they are very dependant on that industry for jobs with the United Steel Workers of America at the various refineries. The Minister indicated that he was going to toughen his stand and ensure that those jobs were retained in Canada. That was very good news.
I am glad that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) happens to be in the House today. I was very concerned when I read an article in the April 21, 1986, edition of NuclearFuel, the main journal of the nuclear industry. The headline is very disturbing to people in the uranium mining communities in Saskatchewan and Ontario. The headline reads: "Canada may drop uranium upgrading policy". The article suggets that Canada is changing is negotiating position on that. The article reads:
The Canadian government is apparently moving to drop its upgrading policy for uranium exports. According to sources, Canadian government officials agreed in principle at a meeting with U.S. officials in Washington April 16 that the upgrading policy should be abandoned. "Both sides felt satisfied," according to one knowledgeable source. He did not say definitely that the upgrading policy

would be abandoned or when, indicating only that the action is "more likely to happen now."
Late last year, the Mulroney Government reaffirmed its commitment to the upgrading policy, which requires Canadian uranium to be exported as UF6 unless there are "exceptional circumstances," such as a customer's prior contract for conversion with a non-Canadian converter-
Although both the Mulroney and Reagan administrations are eager to negotiate a comprehensive free-trade agreement, the discussions of abandoning the upgrading policy are not directly tied to that effort, sources said. Member from Port Hope and the riding of Algoma, and that there will be no secret deals made to trade off that nuclear upgrading policy.

They are world class facilities which can handle some 18,000 tonnes a year. There are about 175 or 180 jobs in Blind River and 340 jobs in Port Hope, a total of approximately 500. The economic activity generated by those two uranium refining and upgrading facilities amounts to about $100 million. There is the additional benefit of $16 million worth of exports. I hope that that will not be walked away from. To trade off those excellent facilities in some secret negotiations, as the report in NuclearFuel of April 21 suggests, would be a very bad action by the Government.
Of course, there is ongoing concern in all of those communities that somehow the uranium refinery and upgrading facilities in Blind River and Port Hope will be traded off in the free trade negotiations. speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many Canadians I have concerns about some of our advanced technology, such as nuclear power. The tragic accident at Chernobyl brings home to all of us that no technology is entirely free of risks.
Before we launch a new and extensive public inquiry we have to look at nuclear power in a comparative way. We have to look at the benefits they bring, such as those that have been enunciated by the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). We must look at the risks, and try to reach a balance.
We must focus on specific situations. The nuclear power program in Canada is different from those in other countries, and in many ways more successful. Nuclear power reactors in Canada achieve a level of safety comparable to the best reactors in the world. They are licensed by an effective independent regulatory agency with expert staff, the Atomic Energy Control Board.
Reactor operators, such as Ontario Hydro, are responsible for the safety of their nuclear plants. They must also convince the AECB that they meet stringent safety requirements before they are allowed to operate those plants.
There are some basic differences between the CANDU reactors and the Chernobyl reactors and the way in which they are operated. I think we need to focus on those differences. The Chernobyl reactor would not meet the AECB safety requirements, and could not and would not be licensed in Canada. The Chernobyl reactor has a graphite moderator which can and did burn. The CANDU reactor has a cool

May 15, 1986
Supply
water moderator which removes heat. In contrast, the Chernobyl reactor does not have a containment building which would satisfy Canadian safety requirements. CANDUs have effective containment.
Nuclear power reactors in Canada embody defence-indepth. All systems must perform to high standards. Major failures are still assumed to be possible, but highly reliable safety systems are included to ensure that, even with those assumed failures, workers and the public are still protected.
An accident identical to Chernobyl cannot happen in Canada. The CANDU reactor is different in many ways from the Chernobyl reactor. Serious nuclear power reactor accidents in Canada are extremely unlikely. The stringent Canadian safety requirements, such as effective containment, ensure that Canadians are adequately protected against accidents. There is always some residual risk with any endeavour, but it is extremely low for the CANDU reactors developed by Canada.
The benefits from our nuclear power program are large, and they more than offset that very small risk. The Government of Canada is fully committed to sustaining the CANDU reactor as a safe, reliable and competitive nuclear power system.
Some critics have noted that the authorities in the Soviet Union told their people that a serious nuclear accident was extremely unlikely, and so these critics asked why we should believe ours when they say the same thing. My response is that the Soviet Union has a highly secretive regulatory practice.

The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) is overreacting to my speech, Mr. Speaker. I should point out to him that for the last six years the AECB has made available, upon request, information dealing with all licensing decisions and the supporting safety analysis, but there has been very little demand for that kind of information.

speechtext:
May I continue, Mr. Speaker? All unusual incidents at nuclear power plants, however minor, are reported to the AECB, and the reports are available to the media and the public, including even the NDP should it ask for them. In the reactor safety field there is an ongoing review to ensure that we work with lessons learned from normal operation and accidents.
Although Chernobyl is very different from the CANDU reactors, Canadian officials will study that accident, along with their international partners, to determine if there are any lessons for Canada. This is one reason why we have requested
information from the U.S.S.R. on the accident. Until we have received more complete information on the causes of the Chernobyl disaster no meaningful review is possible.
A great deal of technical analysis of the accident and its consequences will be necessary before conclusions can be drawn. I am asking the AECB, and other responsible Canadian agencies, to participate in the international assessments of the Chernobyl accident, and to report fully on its implications for us.
The resolution calls for a full and immediate public inquiry into the nuclear industry in Canada. I understand there are serious public concerns about the Chernobyl accident, and we must deal with them in an effective way. The Government has already taken the following steps. It has offered assistance to the U.S.S.R. and extended our sympathy to the victims, while expressing serious concern about the lack of timely information provided. It has ensured that Health and Welfare Canada is monitoring conditions to protect the health of Canadians. It has decided that Canadian reactor safety experts will participate in international reviews on the Chernobyl accident to determine if there are lessons to be learned and applied for Canada. It has requested information from the U.S.S.R. to enable review by Canadian experts.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his colleagues at the recent Tokyo Summit called for international measures to strengthen systems for early warning and mutual assistance in cases of severe accidents like Chernobyl. The Russian proposals yesterday seemed to support these initiatives. We must deal with these problems through international co-operation.
I think these actions speak loudly for the Government's concern and that they represent an appropriate response. The decision to proceed with the public inquiry into nuclear power should properly await the conclusions of the work in progress. The CANDU nuclear power system has already been the subject of two extensive public inquiries, as the Hon. Member for Algoma has noted. The Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning in Ontario, the Porter Commission, found that the CANDU was safe. The select Committee of the Ontario Legislature on Ontario Hydro Affairs found the CANDU was acceptably safe. Parliament and its committees provide an adequate forum for public discussion of issues such as this. The Government in turn will accept its responsibilities and make appropriate decisions. Further public inquiries into nuclear power are not likely to add significantly to our knowledge of the safety of the CANDU nuclear generating system at this time. The Government believes that the system was safe before the Chernobyl accident and it is safe now. Nevertheless, we want to learn as much as possible about the accident, and the proper procedure is for Canada to participate in international studies of the accident and its implications, then to draw the right conclusions and apply them.
I appreciate the concerns of the public about the tragic reactor accident at Chernobyl. We dealt with the immediate
May 15, 1986

consequences of that accident and there is no threat to the health or safety of Canadians. Our own nuclear power program is very different in design, operation, regulation and public scrutiny from that of the Soviet Union. The Government believes that the CANDU reactor is a safe and reliable generating system and that it is properly regulated. We want to learn as much as we can about the Chernobyl accident. We will work together with our international partners to do just that.
Nuclear power has become an important part of Canada's energy mix. We have abundant energy in Canada and most of our electricity comes from hydro power. It is the main source in Labrador, Quebec, Manitoba and British Columbia. We have cheap lower sulphur coal in Saskatchewan and Alberta. Coal from Cape Breton is the main source of electricity in Nova Scotia. These areas may not need nuclear power for many years to come.
In Ontario and New Brunswick, for example, most of the low cost, large-scale hydro power sources are already used. In those provinces, nuclear power is the preferred source. It provides over 40 per cent of the electricity. It saves over $400 million each year compared to the cost of coal. The federal Government has worked with the private sector and with the provinces, especially Ontario, to develop nuclear technology for Canada. The scientists and engineers at Atomic Energy of Canada and Ontario Hydro can be proud of their achievement. The CANDU reactor is a Canadian success story. It uses Canadian technology and resources, adding diversity and security to our energy supply. In today's volatile energy world that is not something to be lightly dismissed.
In Ontario, when the Darlington Station is finished, nuclear power will provide 60 per cent of the electricity for Canada's industrial heartland. Nuclear power helps to keep Canada's electricity costs among the lowest in the industrial world. Electricity is an efficient and productive form of energy and it will continue to increase its share of the energy market. As the Hon. Member for Algoma has already noted, it also provides some 36,000 jobs for Canadians.
Nuclear power is a high technology industry which attracts other advanced industries such as General Motors' proposed $2 billion high tech Autoplex Plant in Ontario. Modern factories need cheap and reliable electricity and nuclear power supplies it in Ontario.
The CANDU reactor is an extremely safe and reliable technology. Ontario Hydro's CANDU's have been among the world's top performers in terms of reliability and electricity costs. Their high performance is not just due to the operational skills of Ontario Hydro. The CANDU at Point Lepreau in New Brunswick was second in performance among over 100 large power reactors in the world in 1985. The CANDU in South Korea was fifth in the world in terms of performance. The CANDU can be operated reliably by smaller utilities as well.
Supply
In most of the industrial countries, nuclear power supplies a larger share of electricity than it does in Canada. The nuclear share is over 30 per cent and increasing in France, Sweden, Belgium, Switzerland, Finland and West Germany. Nuclear power is the leading source of power in Japan. Nuclear power plants in industrial countries displace the equivalent of six million barrels of oil per day. This has been a major factor in reducing oil demand and bringing down the price.
A recent study by the OECD showed that nuclear power was cheaper than coal in most of the industrial countries of the world by a margin of 40 per cent or more. The only exceptions were the western regions of Canada and the United States where coal plants can be built closer to load centres. The industrial countries will have to make sure that nuclear power plants are built and operated safely but they have indicated they are not going to give up that energy option. Nuclear power is here to stay on a worldwide basis.
There have been cases where nuclear power has not worked out well. Some projects in the Unites States have run into cost overruns and some have been abandoned. But many utilities in the United States have very successful nuclear power programs. Like any technology, it has been managed properly, and in Canada we have done it well.
In conclusion, I want to stress that we have a safe, reliable nuclear industry in this country. I do not believe that a public inquiry into nuclear power is useful until such time as we have the product of our reports on the disaster in the Soviet Union.

As well, there are no social institutions which can deal with this technology.
I find that the Minister and spokespersons from the Liberal Party are arrogant in assuming that they, their bureaucracies and our technologies in this country and in others are sufficiently developed that we can place at risk the generations and generations yet to come. Hon. Members have spoken about the Chernobyl accident. Indeed, it is a catastrophe, a catastrophe for the whole human

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point I was trying to make was that it really does not matter very much what type of bureaucracy is in charge of nuclear power plants and development. Whether it is the centrally planned type of bureaucracy found in the Soviet Union or the bureaucracies found in the United States, France, Sweden and the more developed industrialized, technological and democratic societies, the attitude is essentially one of protecting the bureaucracy. Because of this, generally misinformation and lies occur. Reassurances are given by the industry on a continuous basis.
The lesson to be learned from the major accident at Chernobyl is how similar the bureaucracies are and how irresponsible and incapable they are of dealing with nuclear technology. The essential point is the inability of those bureaucracies to deal with nuclear technology. Whether it is the case of the United States, where the low bidder gets the contract, or the case of the bureaucratic state, in which the bureaucracy at times produces unsafe structures, it is all the same.
There was a tremendous amount of hysteria in the western press when the Chernobyl accident first occurred. Again, it is unfortunate that Washington chose to use this as an instrument of the cold war. Certainly Washington was in no position to level the types of charges it did when the accident first occurred.
Now Washington and the international community are condemning the Soviets, and rightly so, for not giving proper information to neighbouring states and for not giving that information fast enough. Again, 1 would ask the same question about Three Mile Island. It took the Americans around three days to inform Congress that a major accident had occurred. It took the United States several days to inform the world that a major accident had occurred. I wonder if the United States ever informed Canada of the danger of a radiation plume moving north and affecting Canadian soil. Certainly Canada is much closer to Three Mile Island than Sweden and Norway are to the site at Chernobyl.
I repeat the point that the bureaucracies and Governments on both sides have shown their irresponsibility and have proven that as a human institution, they are not capable of dealing with nuclear matter.
The other aspect of this accident which makes it so tragic for all of us is the amount of nuclear radiation that has now spread throughout the world. We hear continuous assurances that certain levels of radiation are safe because those levels are compared to what is called the background radiation. They tell us that we are always exposed to radiation, that the rocks and
the soil have radiation and that there is natural radiation. It is true that this natural radiation exists. However, I wonder what the natural radiation level was at the turn of the century before there were above ground nuclear explosions in the testing of bombs and all the nuclear accidents of which Chernobyl is now the latest. The background radiation has increased and the accident in Chernobyl will increase that background radiation even further.
Our generation and the generations to come are guinea pigs. We do not know what effect this accident will have on the health and wellbeing of the world population. I am amazed when I hear members of the Liberal Party and the Minister rise to tell us that everything is all right with the nuclear industry. What gall that these Hon. Members can rise in the House to say that everything is safe while generations yet to come have been placed at risk.
I want to deal as well with the whole question of nuclear proliferation. This is tied very closely to the nuclear industry. We know that Iraq wants its own bomb. In fact, it came pretty close to developing a bomb until it suffered a pre-emptive strike.
When I read about the development of the bomb in Iraq, I found some of the factors involved very interesting. The leverage Iraq used on France and Italy was that it promised those countries a long-term, secure supply of oil in exchange for which it got the nuclear technology. It is interesting to see how this blackmail occurs and how the transfer of material for peaceful uses can very easily be used in the production of war materials.
The case of Iraq is a classic case, but of course Iraq is not the only country involved. Through the use of Canadian technology and our good friends who developed the CANDU reactor, we know that India was allowed to develop its bomb. Pakistan wants to develop its own bomb. Rumours have it that Israel has its own bomb. South Africa wants its own bomb. Brazil and Libya want their own bombs. From where will they get the technology and the material to develop these bombs, if not through companies and countries involved in "the peaceful development of nuclear energy"?
The proliferation of nuclear weaponry is a real threat to the human race. One can only shakes one's head in fright and fear at what the development and usage of nuclear weaponry in the Middle East would do. We are concerned about the effects of radiation in Canada coming from the accident at Chernobyl. Let me tell the House that that accident is child's play compared with what would happen if a bomb were exploded anywhere in the Middle East. It would have effects on the milk and food we eat in Canada, not to mention the hundreds of thousands of people who would suffer and even die in the Middle East, in Europe, and in other surrounding regions.
Another area of concern is nuclear proliferation and how the peaceful use of nuclear energy leads to the use of nuclear
May 15, 1986

material for weaponry. It is a major concern which a public inquiry should address. It should also address what is the nuclear cycle, for example, how uranium mined in Saskatchewan is refined and shipped somewhere else. It should inquire into how the networking occurs and how, on occasion, shipments of these materials become lost or stolen. There are holes in the system through which countries can illegally obtain questionable material, obviously to be used for the production of bombs. It is another area which has to be properly investigated, and hopefully a public inquiry will do that.
I should now like to deal with the economics of nuclear energy. We heard the Minister tell us of the need for expanding nuclear energy. It is the same type of bureaucratic mentality which was supplied to her by her Department and her bureaucrats that overestimated the demand for oil and the price of oil, so that we are now stuck with the many big lemons we will be paying off. It is the same type of mentality as that endless, boundless growth which now saddles Ontario Hydro with billions of dollars of debt and has the entire utility industry in the United States on the verge of bankruptcy. It is bad business planning. Yet from listening to the Minister, no lessons have been learned; it is gung-ho ahead with a mentality which will mean more losses in the future.
I wish to place some figures on the record from the World Watch Institute report of 1986 on how the demand for nuclear energy has diminished. For example, in 1970 the OECD projected that its members would have 568,000 megawatts of nuclear capacity by 1985. The actual total was only about 180,000 megawatts. Plans for nuclear plant construction world-wide levelled off in the mid-70s, and the expected capacity has dropped by more than 100,000 megawatts since 1978. This is largely due to the cancellation of 111 plants in the United States. However, orders have also slowed in Europe, in the Soviet Union, and several Third World countries. The 30 or so U.S. nuclear plants now being completed will have an average cost of close to $3 billion, or $3,000 per kilowatt. The bill for the power they produce will be approximately three times the average wholesale cost of electricity in the United States today.
If we were to decide the fate of nuclear energy just on its economics we would shut it down so fast it would not even be funny. It is amazing that the so-called business-minded Conservatives cannot appreciate the simple fact that the nuclear industry has been a boondoggle. In fact, the estimates are that by the year 1990 the Canadian nuclear industry will have run up a debt of some $60 billion.
Alternatives are available. I am reminded of the statement that if we took the same amount of money it would cost to build a nuclear plant and put it into conservation, we would save more electricity than that nuclear plant would ever produce. However, we have two different lines of development. One is capital intensive. It produces very few jobs. Consumers
Supply
do not benefit, only the banks and utilities benefit. The other choice is to go the soft path to alternate energies and conservation. Consumers benefit from increased conservation and the saving of that electricity. It is not the banks, but it is the consumers or the people. It makes us as people more selfreliant and self-sufficient rather than dependent upon the nuclear industry. It is environmentally much sounder, yet this Government and the Government before it decided for and continues to place its bets on the nuclear industry. It is a shame and a tremendous mistake for which we will continue to pay in the years ahead in terms of a wasted environment, as we have in northern Saskatchewan where uranium is mined, and in terms of ongoing high charges for our electrical power just to pay off the debt. It will be the people who pay, and it will be the banks and the industry which benefit.
A proper inquiry into the cost, the safety, and the whole question of proliferation is urgently needed. I urge Hon. Members of the House to support our motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to the Hon. Member's speech, and I must say that I enjoyed it. I felt it was thoughtful. While I may not agree with all his points, at least he dealt conceptually with the issue. I agree with him that bureaucracies are totally self-serving. It does not matter whether they are in industry or in government, whether they are Tory or NDP, bureaucracies are self-serving.
I want to come back to the motion which his colleagues pointed out was lifted from the Tory campaign promise. It reads:
That this House urges the Government to immediately initiate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power.
Both he and his colleagues have made the point very strongly that they are opposed to nuclear power, the use of nuclear energy, and inferred that the purpose of that campaign statement was to end nuclear energy, and that would be the purpose of the public inquiry. However, let me read the rest of the campaign statement.
We advocate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power and have opened the nuclear power approval process to the public.
We believe that there are good markets for CAN DU technology but that the means of achieving entry into these markets must be re-examined.
We would work with industry and provincial utilities to find new markets in the United States for our surplus electricity.
Since they have taken the first phrase of our campaign statement to infer that our purpose for a public inquiry would be to end the use of nuclear power and, in effect extrapolated it on to our campaign promise, are not the motion and their statements misleading Canadian people?

subsubtopic: DIFFICULTIES ENCOUNTERED BY IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Ontario Council of Agencies Serving Immigrants has drawn attention to some serious shortcomings in the Canadian Jobs Strategy for new Canadians who are unable to take advantage of the various employment programs.
Immigrants are not designated as a target group and the criteria for their participation are highly restrictive. Applicants for job development must be out of the workforce for 24 of the past 30 weeks, while for the job re-entry program they must have been out of work for three years. These mandatory lengthy periods of unemployment effectively exclude numerous immigrants since many of them experience high turnover of short-term work.
The Government should expand its programs to account for the employment reality which faces thousands and thousands of people each year. To ignore this sector of Canadian society is to ignore an integral part of Canada today and the Canada of tomorrow as long as immigration remains a national building force in this country.

subtopic: NORWAY-NEW GOVERNMENT-NINE WOMEN MINISTERS, INCLUDING PRIME MINISTER
NORWAY-NEW GOVERNMENT-NINE WOMEN MINISTERS, INCLUDING PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to offer best wishes to Norway, the country of my ancestors, and to the Democratic Socialist Labour Party Government led by Gro Harlem Brundtland. Gro is a female Prime Minister in a world which has far too few women leaders. She has chosen eight women in her 18 person Cabinet, and there are 30 women in the 71 member Labour Party caucus.
I, and Members of the New Democratic Party, wish Dr. Brundtland well in the difficult tasks which lie ahead. All Members of the House will congratulate Norwegians on being leaders in the western world by bringing women to positions of the highest power and public responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, dynamic, ingenious, honest and efficient, those are the adjectives that come to mind when I think of the small business sector in my riding. Since the 1984 election campaign, I often visit small business people in my riding, and I find those visits very rewarding. Last month, I went from door to door on Plante and Third Avenue, where I was given a warm welcome.
As we all know, operating a small business is not an easy matter. It means working long hours, the competition is intense and risks are high. It is the kind of work that requires a great deal of endurance and tremendous self-confidence. I therefore want to take this opportunity to give them the assurance that they have a colleague here in the Conservative Government and that he is always ready to defend their interests, at any time.
Mr. Speaker, small business people are the cornerstone of our economy, and should be encouraged to pursue their dreams and ideals and make them come true. Again, I want to give them the assurance of my dedication and support. Keep up the good work! The people of Quebec East are proud of you!
Small is beautiful, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is returning from Asia today where he distinguished himself as a true statesman and the best international ambassador Canada has had in a long time.
Over the course of his visit to the Asia Pacific region, a number of significant developments in the area of international trade and economic co-operation were initiated. Among the Prime Minister's many achievements were his commitment from Japan that its building codes would be revised to facilitate exports of Canadian lumber, the signing of a science and technology co-operation agreement, and the opening up of the Korean market to Canadian coal and canola.
These initiatives will be of substantial benefit to Canada as a whole, and to western Canada and Alberta in particular. As an example, the opening up of Korean markets to Canadian coal exports and the slashing of tariffs on canola will inject new vigor in the West's economy. Jobs will be created in the primary production sector, in processing, in transportation, and in many other sectors of the economy.
May 15, 1986

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, the president of the union at the Sorel shipyards informed us of the contents of a letter written by the president of Versatile Vickers to the Hon. Daniel Johnson, a Minister in the Quebec Cabinet, about rationalizing the Sorel yards of Marine Industries. subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PERMIT FISHERMEN TO RESUME FISHING OFF ACADIAN PENINSULA
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT PERMIT FISHERMEN TO RESUME FISHING OFF ACADIAN PENINSULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian fishermen are once again faced with a critical situation with respect to the herring fisheries. The Gulf is full of herring but no fishing is allowed until May 22, since they have already reached their quota and did so in only two days.
Fishermen with over 20 years' experience say there is enough herring to justify doubling the quota.
Fishermen on the northeast shore of New Brunswick should therefore be entitled to continue their operations, which are their sole source of income.
Workers in the fish processing plants are also being deprived of a chance to earn a living. One plant was forced to close after a day's work, while another did so after only two days.
I therefore ask the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to intervene and allow the fishermen to go back to their fishing grounds so they can earn a living.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE FOR CANADIANS TO BUY CARS DESIGNED AND BUILT IN CANADA
IMPORTANCE FOR CANADIANS TO BUY CARS DESIGNED AND BUILT IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since September 1984, 630,000 jobs have been created in Canada, and more than 127,000 in Quebec. Quebec Members intend to continue this trend by promoting the development of our industries.
As part of the strategy for promoting job creation, we urge the Bombardier company to persevere in its efforts to reach an agreement with the Japanese Daihatsu corporation for setting up another automobile plant in Quebec. Such an agreement would help diversify our economic infrastructure and increase our exports.
We therefore urge Bombardier to continue its efforts, and we certainly intend to give the company our full co-operation.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that Canadians will take this opportunity to demonstrate their economic nationalism by buying a car manufactured and designed in Canada.

subtopic: MEMBER'S LETTER TO U.S. AND U.S.S.R. LEADERS
MEMBER'S LETTER TO U.S. AND U.S.S.R. LEADERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read into the record a letter I wrote today to Mr. Ronald Reagan, President of the United States, and Mr. Mikhail Gorbachev, General Secretary of the Communist Party in the Soviet Union. It reads:
Dear Mr. President and Mr. General Secretary:
All citizens of our world can breathe a little easier now that the worst has passed at Chernobyl-just as we breathed easier in 1979 after the Three Mile Island reactor was stabilized.
Marshall McLuhan, a distinguished Canadian, once said that we now live in a "global village", meaning that we all share the problems of nuclear radiation. This goes beyond borders.
Perhaps something really positive can come from the incident at Chernobyl and that you, the leaders of the two world superpowers, can meet to discuss mutual ways of preventing such incidents in the future and of achieving a nuclear test ban.
Both your countries have joined together at Expo 86 in my home city of Vancouver to exhibit your technology to the peoples of the world.
Why not use this occasion to come to Vancouver, Canada in the early Fall to meet on these momentous issues?

May 15, 1986

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada has again announced a reduction in the bank rate.
A few minutes ago, the bank rate was set at 8.59 per cent, which represents a drop of 13 percentage points since last week and 3.79 points since the election in September 1984. The chartered banks have just announced a one-half point drop in the prime rate. Falling interest rates are saving Canadian consumers, governments, businesses, and anyone who has to finance purchases and business operations, hundreds of millions of dollars.
Mr. Speaker, it is a foregone conclusion that this reduction in interest rates will increase consumption and trade. Thanks to our Government's policies, our economic growth is continuing, and we are creating more jobs for Canadian men and women.

maintopic: PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO JAPAN, CHINA, AND SOUTH KOREA
PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT TO JAPAN, CHINA, AND SOUTH KOREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we take the time to read Hansard for the last two weeks, we find very few references to the trip to Asia made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Mr. Speaker, it seems the House, and especially the Opposition parties, had more urgent matters to attend to.
Nevertheless, I think it is important to stress the extraordinary job done by the Prime Minister in Asia. As always, in these circumstances, he has shown he is a worthy ambassador of our country. In Japan, China and South Korea, he had meetings with the highest political leaders, inviting them to invest and buy more in our country. I am sure that in the months and years to come, we will reap the fruit of these meetings.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is returning to Canada this afternoon, after a long and exhausting two-week tour, and I hope that when he returns to the House, all parties will give him a welcome that is, at the very least, respectful and worthy of us as parliamentarians.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF SERVICES ENJOYED BY VOLUNTEER GROUPS
REMOVAL OF SERVICES ENJOYED BY VOLUNTEER GROUPS
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member had asked me to make clear the position of the Conservative Party vis-a-vis its call for a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power. As well, he pointed out that in the position paper they also restated their belief that there were good markets for CANDU technology and that there was some possibility of exporting surplus electric power to the United States. I am concerned about those two aspects, the sale of the CANDU reactor and our technology.
I noted as well that the Conservative statement was somewhat critical of the Liberal Government for selling the Canadian technology to Romania in exchange for Romanian strawberries. I am still concerned about the sale of our nuclear technology to other states. I continue to be concerned about the possible sale of CANDU reactors to Romania, South Korea, Venezuela, Argentina, and all the other places to which our salesmen have gone. Certainly the conditions under which we have made these past sales have been questionable.
As I pointed out in my address, I am concerned about numerous instances in which technology, sold for peaceful purposes, has ultimately been used for the production of warlike materials. A public inquiry should address that question as well.
It is important that we again look at the economics of the nuclear industry, particularly as they relate to sales to the U.S. of our surplus electrical energy. It seems to me that the economics are just not there. For us to get into large-scale production of nuclear power plants in the hope of making some profit by selling the electricity to the U.S. just does not make sense.
In earlier debates, when the Government chose to shut down all the conservation and off-oil programs, I pointed out the per barrel cost of energy equivalents. Venture gas, for example, comes in at $35 a barrel equivalent; Hibernia is $30; Point Lepreau No. 2 reactor is $70 per barrel equivalent. On the conservation side, we have oil which is equivalent to $5 per barrel. I was trying to point out that it is much cheaper to conserve at a cost of around $5 per barrel equivalent rather than going the nuclear route which, at around $70 per barrel equivalent, is the most expensive route. I think it is ludicrous to suggest that we can build nuclear reactors, with their associated problems of waste disposal and environmental protection, and still sell the power produced to the U.S. at a profit. However, if Hon. Members opposite are serious, I plead with them to allow a public inquiry to determine whether these are indeed viable options. Is it viable economically? Is it environmentally safe? Let there be a public inquiry.
One of the things which saddens us is the secrecy surrounding the nuclear industry.
