subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today reads as follows:
That this House urges the Government to immediately initiate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power.
In putting that motion forward, I suppose the mover and his Party intended to put to the test a commitment made by the Progressive Conservative Party during the last election when, I am told, they said that the Progressive Convervative Party would advocate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power and open the nuclear power approval process to the public. That was certainly a substantial commitment. Apparently this is one of many promises that were not kept. In this particular field it is a promise which should not be made lightly, considering the implications and the rising expectations which follow a promise of that kind.
I would have preferred that the mover of the motion had added four words to his motion so that it would read, "That this House urges the Government to immediately initiate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power at home and abroad".
Why do I say that? Because the picture emerging is far from reassuring. There are 26 nations with nuclear power operating a total of some 374 reactors around the world.
As a civilization we have adopted in North America, Europe and other continents, this kind of technology. We must, sooner or later, ask ourselves whether we want to strengthen and accelerate this process, whether we want to examine it, and, if so, what are the options, and whether we want to reduce our dependence on nuclear power.
I would have preferred a motion that had been global rather than limited to the situation in Canada. I do not know whether we can launch an investigation of this kind, ignoring what is happening around us on this continent and in other parts of the globe. Why is that? I am saying that because the recent serious incident in Tchernobyl has demonstrated the consequences of an explosion or a meltdown is such that it affects the global community. It is not like a railway accident or a fire

May 15, 1986
Supply
in an urban centre. It is an event that has far reaching and long-term consequences well beyond the boundaries of the nation where the melt down or accident occurred.
How can we preserve the human race and ensure the health of present and future generations? I must tell you that the present situation leaves very much to be desired. We have created, in an effort through the United Nations in Vienna some years ago, an organization called the International Atomic Energy Agency. That organization was created with a very clear purpose in mind. It was created in order to ensure that nuclear reactors built for peaceful purposes, anywhere in the world, would not be used for military purposes. In that respect I suppose the Atomic Energy Commission in Vienna has performed reasonably well. It has probably fulfilled its mandate, but only within that very narrow scope I mentioned earlier.
The question is, how can we use this existing agency for the protection of health in case of accidents, explosions and meltdowns of this nature in the future? Number one, there are at the present time no internationally agreed upon standards of safety. Every country sets its own standards, and hopefully enforces them, evidently not always with great success, otherwise we would not have had Chernobyl, we would not have had Three Mile Island and we would not have had other known or even perhaps unknown accidents in the history of the nuclear industry.
The question is raised, how do we as a global community develop standards of safety that can be accepted by all nations and become the basic rules of acceptable performance in the nuclear industry all over the world, not just in one country? Secondly, is who is going to enforce them? Although we have the Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna we do not have in that agency the muscle or the teeth required to perform that policing role. Until there is an enforcement agency that ensures that the standards which have been agreed upon are enforced, respected, and put into place, we will be living in an uncertain world. We have 26 nations, as I mentioned to you earlier, with 374 reactors as a global total, each one happily operating independently from the others with different standards, which may be good, but which may also be very shaky, and with no international co-operation to ensure that these operations are safe.
If Chernobyl has taught us anything, it is that whichever nation operates nuclear reactors it has a responsibility to its own citizens, as well as to the neighbouring nations. Otherwise you would not have at the present time, as is the case in Europe, the stopping of cattle and food products at the border between east and west. You would not have grazing prohibitions in some countries until a certain date in the month of May in order to prevent the radiation from moving into milk, and therefore, into the human body. You would not have a number of measures that have been taken in the last 10 days in order to protect health outside the Soviet Union from an event that has taken place inside. You can see the implications and the repercussions that take place in neighbouring nations as a
result of actions taken in one nation and crossing the oceans, so to speak, without respect for boundaries in other continents.
It would seem that an examintaion of the future of nuclear power, limited to Canada, would serve a very limited purpose at this stage, considering how many countries have advanced, considering how many countries have committed themselves, like France, for instance, to having some 400 nuclear reactors in place by the end of the century in order to meet their energy requirements.
There is a global situation here that requires some attention. This is why in recent days I have urged the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), to take an initiative in Canada's name at the UN to see whether there are ways in which we can perform a leading role-considering also the reputation that we have in the global community-in bringing all the interested nations to the table. These should include not only those with nuclear reactor nations, 26 of them, but also the others. We could in this way attempt to produce the regulations and the enforcement standards I referred to earlier as a global initiative. Canada could perform a first class role in this respect. I submit that it has an opportunity to do so. I submit to you that it should also take this opportunity in the name of all those who are very preoccupied, and quite understandably so, as a result of the Tchernobyl event.
That is one observation which comes to mind in reading this particular motion by the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), whom I congratulate for having taken this fine initiative.
The second thought which comes to mind when reading this particular motion is that I would prefer a public consultation, rather than an inquiry, in a forum where over the next couple of years we would consider the future energy needs of Canada, looking at perhaps the year 2020. If you like we could look at the year 2010. The Government of Canada, in an unusually enlightened manner, considering its performance these days, could somehow reach out and say to the public, "We want to know what your thoughts are as to our energy requirements by a certain year?". That would probably correspond with the emergence of a new generation, the youngsters who are now in school.
We would like to know how much we should depend on oil or gas or nuclear energy and how much we should depend on renewable sources, biomass and other sources of energy about which I am not very knowledgeable.
We should somehow focus the attention of the nation on a projected date and eventually, after having carried out public consultation and consultations with various industries and all the sectors interested in energy, the matter will come to rest in Ottawa and the Government would then eventually publish a plan for Canada's energy needs by, let us say, the year 2010. Through that plan we would have an indication of what our requirements are, which would not be a bad thing to know-
May 15, 1986

we do not seem to know it today-and how these requirements should be broken down into the four or five categories I mentioned previously.
I suspect with that kind of consultation, Canadians would be able to tell us as a Parliament and as a Government whether we should maintain our dependence on nuclear energy, whether we should reduce our dependency or whether we should even phase it out. It is quite possible that many interesting ideas would emerge in that process. That has always been our experience when we were in Government whenever we launched a broad public consultation process.
The plan which has emerged in Sweden for its energy requirements by the year 2010-I am just going by memory- has led that country to conclude it should gradually phase out its dependence on nuclear power. That was a wish expressed by the population in consultation with the various sectors. What would happen in Canada? We do not know. However, it certainly has merit as a process, for any democracy at a certain point to look at its long-term requirements and the future and listen to the public about how we should specifically target our requirements by a certain date with respect to oil and gas, nuclear power and renewables such as sun, wind and biomass at large. I think that would be a very healthy exercise and would be very revealing.
I noticed in the Montreal Gazette of May 10 an article by Warren Caragata of the Canadian Press entitled: "Candu reactors are not meltdown-proof'. Mr. Caragata quotes Mr. Domaratski, director general of reactor regulation at the Atomic Energy Control Board, as acknowledging that. He said:
-a meltdown could produce a "catastrophe" involving thousands of deaths.
But he said the risk of a meltdown is so remote, and the chances of major releases of radiation are so small, there's no point in trying to engineer a reactor building to guard against those possibilities.
I learn about these things from the newspapers as does the public and I find statements of this kind a bit unsettling because of the confused message they deliver. I suspect that Canadians at large when they read reports like this would wonder as well. Thank God, so far in Pickering, we have a nuclear plant which has a record of regular performance without accident. The production in Ontario of nuclear power alone corresponds to some 30 per cent of the total requirements of the people in that province.
Over the years, the source of nuclear electricity has become of major importance. We have progressed quite a lot in our dependency on nuclear power in certain parts of the country. But all of a sudden, and I suspect this is the reason we have the motion before us today, the whole dependency on nuclear power has become questionable, and understandably so in the light of the consequences which can be caused by a major disaster. I do not know how well we can change our course of action at this point, having already built what we have built, but certainly we are still in time to determine our future and decide whether we stay where we are without adding to the

number of nuclear reactors, some of which are being planned in some quarters.
Even if we continued with our dependency on nuclear power, we could still begin a policy of gradual reduction of that dependence over the long term, if that is the will of Canadians. That could be achieved if we were to have a sufficiently long span of time. If we do that, we will have to be quite sure of the alternatives on which we will depend. I am told by scientists that in the long term there are opportunities shaping up in the field of energy by way of fission, that technology is advancing in the direction of producing energy by fission. This will permit the production of energy in the quantities we need without having to engage in processes like nuclear power, which are so disturbing in terms of realities.
I would imagine that the nuclear industry at this stage would do itself a great favour if it were to come finally to a conclusion in its research on how to dispose of spent fuel rods. There is a substantial quantity of these fuel rods accumulating at reactor plants in Ontario. This is temporary disposal in expectation of permanent disposition, which is the subject of intensive studies by the relevant authorities. I think the concern of Canadians would be partially allayed if the disposition of spent fuel rods could be resolved soon, so as to at least demonstrate that the industry is capable of disposing of its waste in a proper and environmentally acceptable manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the Hon. Member's presentation. I found myself agreeing with a great deal of what he had to say. I would like his view on the following. With regard to the whole area of nuclear energy we keep hearing from various sources, officials who represent the industry and now, most recently, from the Government, that everything is fine. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) indicated that the matter is being studied, but to date she and her colleagues have confidence in our own nuclear reactors as they operate in Canada.
I could not help but think back to a time, not many weeks ago, in the House when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stood up and said that everything was fine with the two western banks, that the depositors and so on need not worry. He said: "Everything is fine. I am the expert. I am the Minister of Finance and I know these things". The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) then stood up and said: "I am second-in-command here. I have expertise in banking. The banks are sound and stable. There is no worry at all". Even the Inspector General of Banks, the top-ranking public servant in banking matters, said on many occasions: "There is nothing to worry about. These are fine, upstanding, strong and stable banks". Then the Governor of the Bank of Canada stood up and said: "The banks are fine". These were statements made by the most senior financial officials in Canada. They said that our banks, in this case the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, were perfectly sound. They were absolutely and totally wrong.

May 15, 1986
Supply
When we hear officials in the nuclear industry now stand up and say: "Everything is fine and safe, there is no need to worry, we have all safeguards built in", and when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stands up and says: "Everything is fine, we have full confidence in the system", one begins to realize why we are less than confident in their words.
This is what L want to ask the Hon. Member, is not the nuclear industry existing on a whole set of lies in which people say that the industry is, in fact, safe when no one knows for sure if it is or not? This is why we are arguing that, not knowing for sure, we should not proceed to develop such, if you will, a horrible industry in terms of what it can do to humanity. Is this not an industry based on lies, lies from whatever country, at whatever level of the bureaucracy, either here or in other international spheres?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) attributes to me a greater knowledge than I have in my capacity to analyze the industry's qualifications. I am inclined to think that the industry is comprised of professionals who believe in what they are doing. They have produced energy for Canada according to a technology which has its good features and its negative features. Therefore I do not think it would be wise to describe the people in that industry in the way in which the Hon. Member has, although I can understand that he wants to make a point.
The fact is that the industry in Canada is not operating in isolation. There are nuclear reactors which have been built, are being built and which will be built outside Canada, in substantial numbers. While all this is taking place there is no international set of rules on how to protect ourselves as a species while all this is going on. I do not consider this to be a Mephistophelean plan being undertaken by a few evil-minded individuals, but by technicians who are pursuing a certain technology which is available, which mankind has discovered and which-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a brief question to ask of the Hon. Member who gave what I thought was a very good and interesting speech. I am sure he is aware that motion before the House is for Parliament, and in particular for the Government, to consider having a full public inquiry into nuclear power, as was promised during the election campaign. We have heard and seen in the press differing views from different members of the Hon. Member's Party. I would like to know whether the Liberal Party has a solid position in relation to having or not having a full public inquiry into nuclear power.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that at the next convention, which will be held here in Ottawa in November, we will tackle this very important issue. I would also like to add that in tackling it I would like to see it approached as an over-all issue; that is, one with respect to the importance of determining for Canada the elements of an energy plan with a certain date in mind. In this way it can be established how much we want to depend on each of the components within an energy plan, including nuclear, as opposed to singling out one.
Why am I saying this? I think that it is a more productive exercise to look at a distant date. This will make the issue less political, since we do not know who will be in power in the year 2010. Therefore the exercise can be somewhat cooler. It can include the examination of the four or five components which I mentioned, oil and gas, biomass, solar, wind, nuclear and so forth. The Canadian public can be actively engaged in the exercise in an attempt and read what our requirements will be as a total. Then we can break that requirement down by sector and get a reading, a sense of direction from the public that we would consult. I hope that we might be able to do that, although I cannot give the Hon. Member a guarantee that it will occur at our convention here in Ottawa.

In the last 15 or 17 years, the Government of Romania has examined the energy needs of that country. Let us just imagine having lived in Bucharest last winter and having been permitted only one 40-watt light bulb. This was done in order to bring that country's economy into balance with its ability to pay. It is reducing its international debt. In putting themselves through that, Romanians have made a decision, with all of the technology at the disposal of that country and with the Government's capability to negotiate, to acquire the technology which Canadians developed, the CANDU nuclear reactor.
Our visit was coincidental with the accident at Chernobyl. Romania is within the 500-kilometre ring that was uncertain for public safety. Notwithstanding this, that society is totally committed to its need for nuclear energy.
We visited one single site at which four units of CANDU capacity are being constructed at the same time. There is confidence that Canadians and Canadian technology are capable and safe.
Supply
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, having shared in those discussions with the Romanian leaders, that the one thing they were looking for from Canada was the reassurance and reminder that, when dealing with danger, quality control in all its elements, including design, construction, equipment, installation, operation and supervision, will become more and more essential. Canadians working around the world, particularly in such a strange environment as eastern Europe, are looked to with confidence for that kind of quality.
We as a Government are concerned with safety for workers. We are concerned with safety for the public. We are doing this by demanding and rigidly applying all of the standards we have developed along with the Atomic Energy Control Board. It would be very easy to say: "Let's put a moratorium on the nuclear energy industry. Let's close it up. Let's go to some other alternative". However, all of the soft alternatives like solar, wind and wave energy are, as anyone with an engineering background will conclude, very limited resources compared to the demands our society today makes on its energy systems. Low-cost oil and gas is inevitably limited. Alternatives such as coal introduce other environmental concerns and costs.
When Canada shares its advanced, reliable and Canadian developed technology with Romania, Korea or Argentina, we do it with a sense of responsibility. The Government and the business community work together to ensure that the country that is applying that technology will receive our best counsel. We have confidence in our skills and technologies. That includes not simply the front end of the cycle at mining.
I was happy to hear the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) refer to the tremendous uranium mining industry and our ability to refine uranium for the market-place. I will reassure the Hon. Member that it is our policy to refine our resources as much as possible here in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Same old NDP. They talk as if there were not a nuclear energy industry in Canada. A few moments ago, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis) said that Saskatchewan is without any doubt the most richly endowed resource centre for uranium in the world. That is something that has been given to Canada to share safely with the world.
I welcome the opportunity to speak on this opposition motion. It is a motion that allows us to put the facts on the table, and the facts are clear when it comes to the issue of nuclear power in Canada. First, let us look at the differences between Canada's CANDU system and the nuclear systems of the Soviet Union.

May 15, 1986
Supply
Over the past 26 years since Canada entered the nuclear age, the CANDU system has constantly out-performed almost every system in the world, both in terms of generating capacity and safety. Of the 212 large power reactors in the world, six of Canada's 18 CANDUs were in the top 10 in terms of lifetime performance.
Our capacity of 11,000 megawatts exceeds that of the entire James Bay hydro-electric complex and ranks Canada sixth in the world ahead of Great Britain and 15 other OECD countries. Nuclear power met 13.5 per cent of all Canadian electrical demand last year and almost 40 per cent of Ontario's demand in 1985. In other words, we believe that nuclear power in Canada is here to stay.
Nuclear power provides direct employment for 35,000 people. It generates well over $1 billion worth of electricity each year at costs considerably less than the next best alternatives, imported coal or oil.
The Canadian nuclear industry has always been aware of the potential hazards of producing energy from nuclear fission. It has always met the strict regulations of its licensing authority, the Atomic Energy Control Board. As a result, the CANDU nuclear reactor has a safety record virtually unequalled by any other industry. In 133 reactor years of CANDU operation in Canada, there has never been an injury of any kind to a member of the public. There has never been a release of radioactivity of a measurable exposure from any Canadian nuclear station to the public. In over 100 million person-hours of work carried out, no one has been killed or injured through the production of nuclear power.
Since the early 1970s, Ontario Hydro has tried to keep radioactive emissions from CANDU nuclear plants to 1 per cent or less of the regulatory limit set by the AECB.
The AECB annual regulatory limit has never been exceeded, and generally Ontario Hydro has met its self-imposed limit. Regular monitoring shows that radioactive emissions from nuclear power stations are only a fraction of emissions from natural sources and have a negligible effect upon the environment.
A person living on the boundary of a CANDU station would receive only one millirem of radiation per year. This compares with about 100 millirem per year from natural sources. The maximum permissible annual dose for an individual member of the public is 500 millirem.
The CANDU safety approach recognizes that systems and human beings are not perfect. CANDU plant design minimizes the effects of such failings. In practice, good design ensures that an accident is unlikely to occur. This is coupled with strict quality control during manufacture and installation, and with periodic inspection of the major components during the lifetime of the plant.
Information about Canada's nuclear system is widely available. The industry is regulated by an independent body
with an expert staff, the AECB. All unusual incidents at nuclear power plants, however minor, are reported to the AECB, and the reports are available to the media and the public. There is a continuing review of reactor safety to build in lessons learned from normal operation and accidents.
The Chernobyl reactor is different from CANDU reactors. Nonetheless, our officials will study that accident, looking for ways to improve our safeguards.
There are serious public concerns about the Tchernobyl accident. Health and Welfare Canada is monitoring conditions to protect the health of Canadians. Radiation is considered a particular hazard in many peoples' minds, perhaps because of its association with cancer. Critics insist that there is no safe level of radiation; even small doses carry some risk with them. In order to be on the safe side, regulators accept this as true and set their permissible levels accordingly. However, it takes a significant dose of radiation to produce a significant risk of cancer. In the same sense, there is absolutely no safe level of doing anything, even driving to work.
The impact of low level radiation on health is so small that it is very difficult to measure. We all receive a dose of about 300 millirem each year from natural and medical sources. This is much more than the few millirem we could receive each year from living next door to a nuclear plant or a uranium mine.
By comparison, a cross-Canada return jet flight would give an additional dose of a few millirem. This is equivalent to the health risk incurred by smoking a single cigarette. A larger additional dose could be received by simply moving from one location in Canada to another because of the variation in natural radiation background.
Finally, let me come to the question of whether we need a royal commission to investigate all the implications of uranium mining and the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada. There has been a large number of public inquiries into nuclear power in Canada in recent years, and their proceedings and reports have contributed to the information and analysis available to the public.
The Ontario Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning, known as the Porter Commission, published a comprehensive set of reports after five years of work and several million dollars worth of expenditures. The Cluff Lake Board of Inquiry has also reported. These two bodies have taken a very broad view of their mandate and have considered international implications, as well as the moral and ethical aspects of the entire nuclear fuel cycle. In each case they have endorsed the use of nuclear power.
In Ontario a parliamentary select committee on hydro affairs investigated a number of aspects of the nuclear industry-electrical demand, reactor safety, and waste management practices, including the joint Canada-Ontario program for the management of spent reactor fuel wastes and the problem of uranium mine tailings. The committee found that Ontario's nuclear reactors were acceptably safe, thereby justifying the confidence the Government has in the future of
May 15, 1986

the CANDU nuclear industry in Canada and around the world.
Uranium mining and upgrading are important sectors of Canada's great mining industry. After iron ore, copper, zinc, nickel, and gold, uranium is the most important mineral mined in Canada. Canada has a reputation for reliability and quality in terms of its deliveries around the world. We do not only sell the technology which permits the peaceful use of nuclear energy, we also have that great raw material, uranium, which can go into making those plants work. Safe and secure disposal of radioactive waste is a commitment of the Government. We are taking action on this commitment.
On behalf of the Government, I believe that the proposal of the opposition Party for an urgent and immediate study of the nuclear industry is unnecessary at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister seems to make it sound as if he has absolute, total confidence in the Atomic Energy Control Board and in the industry saying that there is nothing to worry about, that no one should blink an eye. Ele and other members of his Party ran on a platform which indicated that they would call for a full public inquiry into nuclear power. I should like to ask the Minister whether or not he agrees with the following quotation. I remind him that he ran on it and was elected on it. In part the book entitled Myth of the Peaceful Atom reads as follows:
The power base of the Canadian nuclear lobby originates in the upper echelons of the AECL and Eldorado. Most of the key figures in the Atomic Energy Control Board (AECB) come from these two Crown corporations, as do most of the top Canadian government advisors on nuclear policy. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the preceding New Democratic Members have pointed out, and as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has been forced to acknowledge, the motion before the House today is taken verbatim from the Progressive Conservative 1984 Campaign Handbook. At page 113 it outlined the Conservative position on nuclear power. It reads:
We advocate a full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power-
We think that was written solely for the purpose of getting elected. When the Conservatives actually got into office they quickly forgot the solemn promises they had made to the people of Canada. They got power for themselves-their only real goal-and everything else went by the boards. Another sacred trust bit the dust.
Why does the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources think we used these words in our motion today? We used them because they are precisely the same words as were in the Conservative campaign promise. We in the New Democratic Party now find ourselves pleading with the Government to live up to the promises it made to the people of Canada. At a minimum, the Government should live up to its promises.
This is nothing new. It seems that Canadians are now coming to expect this kind of dishonesty from the Conservative
Supply
Government. Nowhere has this transparent reneging on campaign promises been shown up more clearly than in the actions of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Immediately after the September, 1984, election, Energy Probe, the Toronto-based watch-dog group which has for years vigorously monitored energy policy development in Canada, wrote to the Minister to encourage her to follow through with her Party's clearly enunciated promise to launch a "full public inquiry into the future of nuclear power". The Minister rebuffed Energy Probe.
My colleague, the Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper), then took up the cause of Energy Probe, and on April 1 of last year wrote to the Minister of Energy requesting yet again that the Conservatives honour their promise to have a "full public inquiry into the nuclear industry". That was on April 1. Perhaps the response of the Minister was more akin to an April Fool's joke. She replied:
I (do) not intend to broaden my consultations beyond the industry and the provinces in order to arrive at a decision on this matter. I have consulted with these sources and it is my view that a national inquiry on this topic is not a high priority at this time.
That is a complete reversal. It is a complete and total repudiation of the promises on the basis of which the Conservatives had made their grab for power only a few months before that. This is a sorry track record. We had hoped that perhaps the events of the last few weeks in Ukraine, to which the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton) has just alluded, might have impinged upon the Minister's consideration of what constitutes, in her words, "a high priority at this time". The disaster at Chernobyl, and the even greater catastrophe of a reactor core meltdown which was so narrowly avoided there, has driven home to all sane people the horrendous dangers inherent in reliance on nuclear power.
The Minister of Energy talked about risks. There are risks in everything in life. There is the risk of getting hit by a car when you walk across the street. Look at the risks of having a reactor meltdown in Pickering or somewhere like that. It means death for the people around Toronto. You die.

Those who watched The Journal on CBC television a couple of weeks ago may recall an interview with a British nuclear scientist who observed in this connection that the top Soviet leadership had reacted with considerable dispatch once they had been fully acquainted with the nature and import of the problem. He, of course, defined the problem as the bureaucracy, the politicians and leaders getting to know the extent of the problem because they must go through various levels of bureaucracy. This is a phenomenon which we have in Canada. A couple of Members on both sides of the House have alluded to that in this debate.
It was suggested that we were doing something bad when we raised the secrecy of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the Atomic Energy Control Board. This is an account of a meeting in Moscow by American Congressman Michel of Illinois who was talking to the Soviets. Michel said:
-the Soviets do not plan to curtail construction of their nuclear power plants, which they feel are safer than those in use in the United States.

speechtext:
They told us they had safe plants and that they would not have an accident. Is this not the same kind of stuff that we are hearing from the Government today? Make no mistake, we do not want to have a nuclear accident, but we want to ensure that it does not happen in Canada.
We are having this debate today because in this way the Canadian public can see the dangers. People in my constituency are afraid of the rain that is falling. People in Ottawa were afraid of that. There are real fears. They are examining food in Europe. This is the time for the world to think about what is going on. While we are talking about the much vaunted superiority of the North American nuclear reactor design we should recognize that it is generally acknowledged that the Three Mile Island reactor came within a half hour of suffering a full-scale reactor core meltdown. I quote John Swaigen, an environmental lawyer from Toronto who said:
There are many uncomfortable parallels between the situation in the Soviet Union and in Canada. Both are Arctic countries with similar climates. Both have nuclear facilities sited near major cities.
Our scientists assure us that our nuclear plants are safe. So did theirs. In this field at least we share the Soviet Union's preoccupation with secrecy.
There is a reactor in Hanford, near the Columbia River in the State of Washington, just south of British Columbia. I raised this in the House today. It is a graphite reactor like
May 15, 1986

Chernobyl. It is uncontained like Chernobyl. It is 40 years old and has been described by Dr. Rosalie Bertell, a research scientist and consultant to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, as an accident waiting to happen. She wants to have this reactor closed. She says it is "so old anything can happen". I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs about this today. He did not even know that his Department had been talking to the Americans about this reactor. Those are the kinds of things we would like to see in the inquiry. Are we prepared for a disaster in Canada? Are we talking to the Americans about their old reactors? Are we looking into the safety of our reactors as well as theirs? Are we looking into the burial of spent fuel? Are we looking into the dangers of low radiation tailings, as my friend from Skeena pointed out? How much are we paying for these reactors? What are the alternatives? Can we get into energy conservation? All these questions need to be addressed.
The NDP have put forward other Bills on this subject. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) put forward a Private Members' Bill to establish a moratorium on the continued development of nuclear power in Canada. We have been trying consistently to get a full inquiry into this matter.
I want to reply to something raised by some Conservative Members. They have said it is going to be difficult to take us out of the nuclear system. I agree that some hard decisions will have to be made. Jobs are on the line. Scientific prestige is on the line. However, leadership means that you have to face these kinds of decisions. There are other answers. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) talked about alternative jobs involved in cleaning up the tailings and decommissioning the plants. Working people do not have to be put out on the street. Sweden has had to face this problem. Like Canada, Sweden has developed a reliance on nuclear-generated electricity. As a matter of fact, over 40 per cent of Sweden's electricity is currently nuclear generated. In Canada in 1983, it was about 12 per cent to 13 per cent. Sweden is far more heavily dependent than Canada on nuclear power, and any movement away from nuclear power would cause far greater economic dislocation than that facing Canada.
In saying that, I take into account the severe impact such a decision would have on particular regions of the country. I fully recognize that Ontario projects that by 1990 nearly 60 per cent of electricity produced by Ontario Hydro will be nuclear generated. However, I think the Swedish experience is directly applicable to Canada, particularly Ontario. In Sweden the major commitments to proceed with nuclear power were made between 1956 and 1970. Then questions emerged as to the wisdom of doing this. A public debate ensued. That culminated in 1980 with a national referendum in which the Swedes decided to abandon nuclear energy. This, of course, is the reason the Government is afraid to have an inquiry. The powers that be do not want an inquiry that would lead to a public debate which might in turn lead to the Canadian people doing something about nuclear power.
Supply
As a result of that referendum, the Swedish Parliament set up guidelines for the phasing out of nuclear-generated power. The guidelines stipulated that no further construction of nuclear reactors would be undertaken beyond the 12 existing or under advanced construction at the time. The last reactor would be taken out of service by no later than 2010, after an estimated operating period of 25 years. They set a sunset period. A National Board for Spent Nuclear Fuel was also established to oversee the management and disposal of waste generated by the Swedish nuclear program up to its termination. They have tried to start dealing with nuclear waste. An important consequence of this decision is that by limiting the nuclear program in time and size, the Swedes also set limits for nuclear waste production.
The importance of the Swedish experience in providing some guidelines for Canadian nuclear policy lies in the thorough technical follow-through which they have constructed to deal with the fallout of these fundamental policy changes. Even before the 1980 referendum their Parliament had passed, in 1977, a Stipulation Act under which permission to load a nuclear power reactor for the first time can be given only if the owner had shown that the spent fuel could be quite safely disposed of. After the referendum the Swedish Parliament unanimously passed, in 1981, a law concerning the financing of future expenditures for spent nuclear fuel. In this legislation, in which the main principles for the present day Swedish waste management policy were laid down, they dealt with the planning and financing not only of long-term waste management, but of the ultimate decommissioning of existing nuclear reactors. That is what my friend from Skeena was talking about.
What are the lessons for Canadians that emerged from the Swedish experience? How does that experience relate to the motion before us today? First of all, we in the NDP recognize that decisions must be made in the real world where major shifts in energy development cannot occur overnight. However, at some point a first step must be taken if somewhere down the road we are to arrive at a desired destination. That is all we are asking for. A first step by this Government was promised two years ago, which it has not yet taken, and which, according to the Minister's statement today, it is going to continue to postpone on the flimsiest of pretexts, that of an inquiry into the future of the industry. Can you believe the gall exhibited by the Minister's position? A campaign promise ought not to be dealt with because an event totally unforeseen when the promise was made, the Chernobyl disaster, has not been fully reported on. That is ludicrous. Who does the Minister think she is kidding with this trite, facile evasion?
I want to conclude by replying to the speech of the Minister of State for Mines. He is a decent man and he gave a decent speech. He raised the question of why are we not up-to-date. I think we are really up-to-date. I think the issues in the 1990s are going to be health, peace, environment, leisure, and technology. Who is out of step? I think we are in step. We are dealing with those issues today. We are not asking for the

decommissioning of all the plants. We have suggested the way the Swedes have dealt with the problem. We are not asking to even stop the expansion of reactors. We are simply asking the Government to live up to its campaign promise, which was that there would be an inquiry into the future of nuclear energy. After Chernobyl, I cannot think of any inquiry which is really more essential than this particular one. 1 cannot think of anything. The Conservatives are just not listening to the Canadian people. In the past three years, new evidence indicates survivors were exposed to less radiation than previously believed. Ever since the early post-war years, scientists have been meticulously recording the development of cancer and other diseases among the 80,000 survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Scientists have been relating cancers to the doses that the victims received. The original estimates of those doses are now recognized to be too low, which means that the cancers observed were caused by lower doses than originally thought.
Doctor Edward Radford, Chairman of the U.S. National Sciences Committee on the biological effects of ionizing radiation, said that the radiation risks are at least 10 times worse than generally accepted. In terms of the radiation levels alone, aside from the other questions of safety-here I am talking about the safety of the workers that the Minister of State for Mines claims to represent so carefully-here is evidence from the U.S. National Sciences Committee saying that our level of risk in Canada is perhaps 10 times higher than the AECB is prepared to admit. If the Hon. Member had stayed at the conference and listened to the Minister's speech, he probably would have learned something. This Government wholeheartedly supports the conservation end of things. But we also support the nuclear industry because it plays a very important role in our energy mix. The NDP tells us not to burn coal because it creates acid rain, not to burn oil because it is disappearing, not to dam up any more rivers because we flood much needed land, not to do all this. That is fine, but where does our power come from? One of the advantages of Ontario, and Quebec for that matter, is an abundance of cheap power. That is why industries are attracted to Ontario. They know the energy is there and they know it is cheap. Forty per cent of Ontario's power is generated by nuclear energy, soon to be 60 per cent. That is very important for the economy of Ontario.
I would like to list the studies of the industry which are going on: the Environmental Assessment Review on New Brunswick's Point Lepreau nuclear generating station, and the Federal-Provincial Environmental Assessment Review on Point Lepreau; the National Energy Board hearings on the export to the U.S. of electric power from Point Lepreau; the Royal Commission on the Health and Safety of Workers in Mines, Ontario's "Ham Commission"; the Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning, Ontario's "Porter Commission"; La Commission Parlementaire sur I'Energie, Quebec's "Joron Commission"; the select Committee on Ontario Hydro Affairs; the Cluff Lake Board of Inquiry, Saskatchewan's "Bayda Inquiry"; the Ontario Environmental Assessment Board hearing into the expansion of uranium mining at Elliot Lake; the Committee on Nuclear Issues in the Community, a cross-Canada effort by the Science Council and Royal Society; five hearings under Canada's environmental assessment and review process regarding a proposed uranium refinery, four in Ontario and one in Saskatchewan; the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Uranium Mining in B.C., the "Bates Commission"; the Energy Committee of the New Brunswick Legislature; the Key Lake Uranium Mine hearings in Saskatchewan; the Northwest Territories legislative hearings into uranium exploration and mining, and the uranium inquiry under Judge McCleave in Nova Scotia.
Hearings into Canada's domestic nuclear industry were arranged by a group of churches in Toronto, completely independent, at the end of 1984. That group is not known to be the greatest supporter of nuclear energy. An impartial panel heard evidence from both sides. It was a good hearing. We followed it very carefully. It concluded that nuclear power was an important and viable option among the available energy resources.

This industry has been studied to death. We are concerned about what happened at Chernobyl. I believe all thinking people are concerned about that. To compare the Chernobyl incident with what could happen in Canada is like comparing apples with oranges. The process at Chernobyl is an entirely different one. It does not have the safety features built in. The Hon. Member has stood up and said that the Soviets told us that it was safe. He knows the system of Government there. He knows how the public is informed there-they are not informed. The accident was not reported until three days after it occurred. The only reason it was reported was because it was being monitored by another country and that other country blew the whistle. So, to compare what is going on in Canada with what is going on in the U.S.S.R. is completely unfair. The Hon. Member knows that. It is a red herring.
He is right when he says that at one time in Canada everything was secret. I agree with him, I too think it was a mistake. It was a mistake on the part of Atomic Energy of Canada and on the part of the Atomic Energy Control Board.
I think it was a mistake on the part of the Government of the day. Today, I think the industry realizes that it was a mistake. It was foolish to try to keep these matters from the public. The public has every right to know what is going on. It has every right to try to understand the complexity of the industry.
I have been involved in this sector rather intimately for the past year and one-half. I think I have learned a great deal from it and about it. It is a very complex issue. Today, everything is public. The reports of the AECB are public. If there is the slightest incident, no matter how minor, it is immediately reported to the press and to the public. We have seen these reports come out from time to time when it has been necessary to close down a reactor because of a leaking valve or whatever.
I agree with the Hon. Member when he says that at one time the situation was not satisfactory. But today, thank God, it is. Thank God that the Governments and the control boards are open with the public. People fear the unknown and that is a fact. The more open and honest we can be with the public, the more information and facts we can give to show that all possible safety precautions are being taken in regard to this valuable industry, the less fear there will be.
Members opposite have talked about Argentina. I can tell Hon. Members that the CANDU reactor in Argentina is under the strict control of the International Atomic Energy Board. It keeps a close eye on the situation. We do not or will not deal with a country unless a non-proliferation agreement is signed. The reactors are for peaceful purposes.
The countries to which I have travelled, and those which are interested in the nuclear option, are starving for power. One of the main problems is that they do not have enough power; they cannot get it. Romania was also mentioned earlier. The Romanians have been pumping oil for 70 years and the

We should assure ourselves-and to date I am assured-that we have all the safety requirements built in to our CANDU system which can possibly be built in.

I am not sure of how much time I have left, Mr. Speaker, since I did not keep an eye on it. I have covered conservation and the study of the industry. I now wish to talk about safe storage for the waste from the nuclear industry.
There are three federal programs under way in Canada concerning the storage and disposal of radioactive wastes. These programs are related to three different types of radioactive wastes produced in the country, namely, irradiated fuel wastes, uranium mine tailings and low level radioactive wastes. The goal of these programs is the eventual transfer of the wastes from the current storage mode where their safety is assured by means of active monitoring and control. Since there were all sorts of innuendoes that there is not safe storage today, I can tell Hon. Members that there is safe storage on site at the generating stations. It is monitored on a minute-byminute basis. There is enough room at those sites to store all wastes produced for the next 75 years. However, we are not happy with that. We are proceeding with these programs to assure the long-term safe storage for waste from the nuclear industry.
The major program deals with the irradiated fuel wastes. It is a co-operative research and development program with the Province of Ontario and the United States. It is budgeted at a current level of some $37 million per year. The program is managed by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited Whiteshell Nuclear Research Establishment in Manitoba. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway knows that there is an open invitation to him and his colleagues on the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources to visit the site and to see the work going on. The disposal concept being assessed in this program is the burial of the fuel wastes 500 to 1,000 metres deep in the crystalline rock of the Canadian Shield.

The final AECB regulatory requirement was issued in January of 1985, and a second set of concept assessment documents from AECL was released in 1985. The final set is to be released in 1988 at which time the concepts are to be evaluated by: an inter-agency review committee, including staff representatives of the Atomic Energy Control Board, Environment Canada and the Ontario Ministry of the Environment; public hearings; the AECB; and the Governments of Canada and Ontario.
Approval of the concept by all of these bodies represents a full acceptance of the concept. Such acceptance, together with a decision by the owners of the irradiated fuel to actually implement disposal, is required before site selection for a commercial repository can be started. The July 1985 concept assessment document concludes that the total occupational risk, radiological and conventional, associated with the construction, operation and decommissioning of a disposal facility will be no greater than the risk in comparable industries.
While the main focus of the report is on evaluating the possible risks due to the facility, a part of the analysis also addresses the potential benefit to a variety of community types. The report states that an increase in employment and in

the economic base generally would be beneficial to every type of community. There would be direct, indirect and spin-off employment. In addition, revenue in the form of property taxes or grants in lieu of taxes would be generated for community development purposes.
I do not wish to take advantage of the time that was given to me by the Opposition and for which I am grateful. However, I would like to sum up that particular part by saying that the Canadian program is held in high regard internationally. It supports the collective opinion of the experts in the nuclear energy agency of the OECD. They said that there is a high degree of confidence in the ability to design and operate geological disposal systems which will assure long-term isolation for high-level waste or spent fuel and meet the relevant long-term safety objectives.
I mentioned two other programs. Briefly, the second program initiated in 1983 deals with uranium mill tailings. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. Provided that I do not need too much filler time, I will not get into what I think is the red herring part of the debate-the PC handbook and the broken promises which were made during the last election campaign. Frankly I think Canadians have come to expect that the Government will never live up to the promises it made in the election campaign of 1984. I do not think reference to that red herring will do much to enlighten the Canadian public in respect of the motion before the House.
All three political Parties recognize that the major catalyst which led to the present debate on the floor of the House of Commons was the nuclear reactor disaster at Chernobyl. All of us would agree that the events following that disaster have made us aware of the need for a co-ordinated international plan of action to deal with this kind of crisis in the future. It goes without saying that we live in a very interdependent world. It is not only an economically interdependent world. In terms of the ecological system, clearly it is a world which is so fragile and interdependent that we can no longer afford to have take place in the future what took place in the immediate days and weeks surrounding the disaster at Chernobyl.
Even to this day I find it difficult to believe that an international power, namely the Soviet Union, would be so irresponsible that it would not inform its other world neighbours of the potential harm to the atmosphere and the ecolology as a result of that nuclear reactor disaster. It was almost as if the Soviets hoped that the high radiation levels which would be emitted into the atmosphere would never be detected. It is incredible, in the year 1986, that any country would attempt to throw a blanket of misinformation over a nuclear disaster of that magnitude.
The fact that it took a Swedish Government Ambassador to approach the appropriate authorities in Moscow to determine if any nuclear accident took place speaks volumes for the problems and the way in which the Soviet Government went about dealing with the disaster.
I should like to refer to the fact that it took several days for our own Government to respond. I say with all sincerity that the Department of National Health and Welfare has done what was expected of it and with the resources available to it in an attempt to cope with the repercussions from the nuclear accident at Chernobyl. As the House will recall, in the days
Supply
following the accident, warnings were issued by the Department of National Health and Welfare concerning rain-water and concerning the uptake of radiation in our food supply or cycle. This illustrates the problem in an interdependent world when a nuclear accident occurs.
It simply cannot be contained within the area immediately surrounding or adjacent to the reactor site. It pointed at the weakness of the international agencies in responding to that kind of an emergency. Last night I witnessed the normal reaction among people in the free world. There was a two or three minute segment concerning the American doctor, I believe from the State of California, whose specialty is bone marrow transplants. He recognized that neither the Soviet Union nor anywhere else in the world could cope with a disaster of the magnitude of Chernobyl. On his own volition, together with a number of U.S. companies, the doctor managed to get together 136 bone marrow transplants for transfer to the Soviet Union. The expertise made available by that physician and his team speaks volumes for the way in which Canadians or any free thinking intelligent person would respond.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) made a statement in the House. I believe my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), responded for the New Democratic Party and I responded for the Liberal Party. We both talked about the need to improve the response plan to a disaster at the international level and at the national level here in Canada. That is where the focus of debate should be.
The use of nuclear power will increase in the future. When one looks at the industrial giants, such as Japan, one has to come to the conclusion that nuclear power will be part of the energy options that will be made available to them. As long as that is the case, there exists the potential for disaster, similar to Chernobyl.
As a country that has played a significant role in the development of nuclear energy, we must take a leadership role. The international community must be in a much better position to respond to disasters like Tchernobyl.
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare made his statement, I said that I thought we should be doing more than warning Canadian citizens in the immediate vicinity of Chernobyl. Canada should be taking a leadership role at the international agency in Vienna that deals with nuclear power and issues. We should be telling the Soviet Ambassador here in Canada in very strong terms that Canadians deplore and will not stand for the kind of misinformation the Soviet Union attempted to dish out in the days following the disaster. With respect to the defence ramifications of how we view the Soviet Union, outside of the NATO pact and the Warsaw pact, the Soviet Union, whether we like it or not, is a member of the international community. We deal with the Soviet Union at the United Nations and on a bilateral basis.

May 15, 1986
Supply
We should be speaking openly to the Soviet Government about how we feel it mismanaged the Chernobyl crisis. The Soviet Union must realize Canadians were upset that it took Soviet authorities seven to eight days to inform the international community about the disaster. We have learned since then, even after the Soviet authorities acknowledged the existence of the problem at Chernobyl, but refused to acknowledge the severity of it, that until five or six days ago the Russians were still in danger of having a meltdown, an out of control reactor disaster, and yet their authorities still did not ask the international community for aid.
If we are going to have nuclear energy as an alternate source of energy in my future and my children's future, we should be asking Governments at the international level to have plans of action. We need international medical teams and international nuclear experts ready to respond to whatever country is in trouble. Canada has been at the forefront in the development of nuclear energy. I am sure Canadians would want the Government to lead that kind of a discussion at the international level.
I believe the Chernobyl disaster points out the inadequacies of many of the existing response programs we have in Canada. The Minister of National Health and Welfare responded. He told us he had established a special task force to review the procedure of dealing with disasters of the same magnitude as Tchernobyl. We need programs to deal with crises in the nuclear energy field. We should make sure that at the end of this exercise of review we can as a Government assure Canadians that we have done everything possible to deal with a nuclear crisis in the event of one.
I come from an area of the country that has and will maintain an economic interest in nuclear energy. I do not represent the City of Elliot Lake. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), has that honour. In the years from the mid 1950s into the 1960s and 1970s, the advent of the nuclear industry led to a significant economic improvement for those people on the north shore.
I recall very well the debate on the location of the El Dorado refinery when the decision was made to put the refinery in the Blind River area adjacent to Elliot Lake. Even our own Liberal Government at the time was considering putting the Eldorado refinery in southern Ontario in the Port Hope area. I recall the discussions we had with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources at that time. We told him as a northern Ontario caucus that if we were going to have nuclear energy, then surely the resources mined in northern Ontario should be refined in the North. That was our basic argument. We were successful in making sure the economic spin-offs to that industry were concentrated in the area of the resources.
As you can recall, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government became involved in the nuclear field in the 1940s. This was done in a joint effort with the United States. It began with a military application of the use of nuclear energy. Since that time, nuclear technology has been used by nations to deal with their energy requirements. Nuclear technology is used in
medicine, and in altering the ways in which we view our world. There have been some very important spin-offs to the advent of the use of nuclear technology since its inception some four decades ago. Even the Province of Saskatchewan, held successively by New Democratic Governments for several decades, recognized the need for alternate uses of energy, as does the present Government in Saskatchewan.
Any person who objectively and intelligently addresses the issue of nuclear power recognizes it as a form of technology that creates energy. We are asking to make sure that the energy choice is done in a safe way. That is the issue. I do not think we can hide our heads in the sand and with the wave of a magic wand eliminate nuclear power stations in Canada. That is simply not going to happen. Considering the percentage of hydroelectricity in the province which is generated by nuclear stations, it is obvious that the province has a vested interest. If the Province of Ontario has a vested economic interest, so has every citizen of the province.
I do not think we should be focusing on the elimination of nuclear energy as a source of power. We should be focusing research and development on technology to deal with the waste products of nuclear energy. The debate should be focused on the need for safe maintenance and operation of nuclear plants in the country. The Canadian public demands and is entitled to resources at all levels of government to respond in the event of an emergency. That is where this debate should be focused.
If people, for one moment, believe that that is the proper way to approach the issue of nuclear energy, then we must direct more and more resources toward the research and development in the three areas about which I have spoken. That must be the commitment of any government. Regardless of what political party sits to the right of the Speaker, those are the issues with which it will be faced when in government.
The one area with which I have some dispute is the cut-back in R and D which occurred after the 1984 election. The people of the riding of Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke have a right to be upset. I am speaking of the people who are involved in the nuclear industry and live in that riding. They had a right to believe that the proper amount of R and D would be done. The questions which are asked by the Canadian public deserve answers. If the debate is focused in that area, it is a justifiable debate. However, to engage in rhetoric by talking about another broken Government promise takes away from the level of debate which the public deserves to hear in the House of Commons.
Those are my thoughts with respect to this issue. I am sure that in the last 10 days to two weeks, due to the magnitude of the disaster at Chernobyl, all Canadians have had cause to rethink their concerns about the use of nuclear power. I think they would like to have their representatives here in the House of Commons debate the issues in the areas which I have outlined. The public needs those answers. I have listened to some of the debate here this afternoon, albeit not much. I
May 15, 1986

could not be accused of that. In order to have a full debate about the use of nuclear energy, alternate uses of power must be put into the equation.
The Liberal Party has not committed itself to nuclear power, but it has committed itself to ensure that the proper safeguards are in place for the maintenance and use of nuclear power. The Liberal Party is committed to the improved use of moneys for research and development into methods for handling waste products. Those long-term answers are required in order to live comfortably with nuclear energy. To my knowledge, there is no form of energy in the world which does not have some malicious side effects. If we were to remove suddenly all of the energy power stations in the world and replace their energy output with energy derived from coal, the result would be a problem with the atmosphere. Every form of energy has problems. The debate must be intelligent and informed. If we can achieve that, I think we will have advanced the debate which the people have so badly wanted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a short comment and put a question to the Hon. Member about nuclear power.
Naturally, the Hon. Member has denounced the delay of the Soviet Union in informing its own population and the other countries which are now affected, and this includes Canada, albeit not too seriously.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member why it is usually the leftist groups who organize protest marches against nuclear energy, and especially against the United States and other countries of the free world. How does the Hon. Member explain the fact that there were so few demonstrations in this case? Where are all the leftist groups which are gaining ground in nearly all parliamentary institutions, especially in Europe? Where are they? How can the Hon. Member explain their reaction to the events in the Soviet Union?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not have any problem with the question asked by the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin), but I do have one in trying to explain the absence of many people who do not want nuclear power in this country.
In view of the urgency of the situation, I think that everyone in this case wanted an answer to a two-part question. First, internationally, they wanted an answer by the international community about the problem in the Soviet Union. Second, in our country they want to see the development of an emergency plan of action in case of a similar problem. I think that in this case the response of people the world over was indeed to obtain the necessary information concerning the crisis created by the Soviet Union.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY-NUCLEAR POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in this debate and to conclude it. The motion before us this afternoon, which calls for a public inquiry into nuclear power, is one of enormous
Supply
importance to the well-being of the entire country and, potentially, to the good health of individuals and communities in selected parts of our country where nuclear power is already important.
Nuclear power as an energy source deserves recognition for the enormous dangers which are inherent in that industry. We have all been watching, with a horrible fascination, the unfolding of the disaster at Chernobyl in the Soviet Union. We wonder what its consequences will be. One hardly need point out to people-although in the debate which we are having this afternoon it is worth doing-that when a disaster occurs at a nuclear power plant, it will not lead only to a loss of energy for people in the immediate area. It is not something which will affect only those persons who are in the plant in the way of immediate consequences of the accident. It is not a matter of physical injury and that is that. Quite clearly what happens or can happen in one of these disasters is a spreading of potential death for large numbers of people at considerable distances from the reactor itself. What the consequences are for those people beyond the immediate vicinity of the plant is something that only time will tell. It will take statistical studies to clarify the consequences.
What is so often forgotten when considering these things is that the question of safe levels of radiation is not a subject on which there is agreement in the scientific community. We live with the standards of the 1940s and 1950s. We live with the thought that it is high levels which are dangerous. Yet there are sneaking suspicions among some epidemiologists and other researchers that quite low levels of radiation can have equally harmful effects in the long term on human beings. The effect on workers in the plants, the effect on thousands of people at some distance from the plant, the spreading of radiation around the globe, the warnings not to drink rain-water even though it is safe for children to splash around in it, the need to check for radiation levels in milk, all underscore the fact that we are dealing with a quite unusual form of energy.
We take comfort from our technology. We have been fortunate in the Western hemisphere in not having any of our nuclear plants affected by earthquakes or similar disasters. Yet what would happen to that technology in the event of that kind of disaster? How widely would the consequences be felt? It is for those reasons that my colleagues and I are emphasizing the importance of a public inquiry on nuclear energy. I suggest that the need to do this can be underscored by the fact that we have built societies and developed economies on the basis of two kinds of dubious energy, the first being petroleum and the second being nuclear energy. Dependence on petroleum has made it possible for the producers to shock our economies and bring us near the brink of economic disaster several times. Because of the failure of their price program recently, there is the possibility of a new kind of disaster. We are in a most perilous economic situation these days because of our petroleum-dependent economy.
13344

May 15, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Then we have the consequences of dependence on nuclear energy which has developed in some parts of Canada. I am a Member of Parliament from Ontario and it has already been suggested by others that Ontario Hydro is a major user of nuclear energy. It is worth underscoring the importance of that dependence. In Ontario, 40 per cent of the energy being used is nuclear-generated. That 40 per cent is the base of the Ontario Hydro system. The reason is quite simple. Nuclear energy is a form of energy best used at a steady rate over long periods of time. It is much easier to control hydroelectric facilities by shutting off the water at night and then lifting the gates when morning comes and the energy is needed. It is relatively easy to fire up thermal plants of one sort or another. They are used as supplements.
What is running day and night, week after week, year in and year out, are the nuclear power plants which provide the base. The other power sources are called in as required to meet the demands of industry and the ordinary consumer. That is the reality in this province. As a Member of Parliament from northwestern Ontario, living on the Canadian Shield in an area on which Atomic Energy of Canada has fairly obvious designs for burying its waste, I appreciate the opportunity to address this matter.
There are so many aspects of the use of nuclear energy by Ontario Hydro that it boggles the mind. Surely planting those great stations so close to Metropolitan Toronto has to be an act of corporate lunacy. The cynics, or the tough-minded, I am not sure which they are, or the merely stupid, say that if it is going to be the basis for Metropolitan Toronto's power supply, then let the plants be close to hand rather than far away. I suppose suggesting that it should be in the Bruce-Grey Peninsula or somewhere up there-
