ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-NIAGARA RIVER-TOXIC CHEMICAL DUMPS SITES. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to put the intervention tonight in the proper context, I would like to cast your memory back to October, 1984, when the Niagara River Toxic Chemical Committee produced a report on toxic chemicals and emissions into that water body. In May of 1985, the then Minister of the Environment made a glowing promise about obtaining from the United States Government a plan of action for the clean up of emissions, particularly the toxic chemical emissions, into Lake Ontario. It was quite a commitment that the then Minister made. It raised our hopes. I was pleased to hear that because it indicated that the then Minister intended to take pretty vigorous action and to make the United States authorities realize that there must be, on their part, an action that would enforce the commitment they made with us when they signed the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement in 1978.
In October of 1985, when the head of the Environmental Protection Agency visited Ottawa and submitted a report, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) was fuming and very upset over a criticism that was levelled by me because he felt I had not seriously approached and studied the proposal that had been brought here to Ottawa. The fact is that that proposal was kept secret in Canada and was made available
May 15, 1986

south of the border. I had to rely on whatever information I could get to express my views on that.
My views at that time were fairly consistent with what the Minister himself said in March of 1986 in the House of Commons, which triggers this exchange tonight. I am quoting from page 11809 of Hansard. In answer to a question, the Minister of the Environment said the following:
I did state categorically on behalf of the Canadian Government that we think the only solution for the disposal sites on the American side along the Niagara River is excavation and incineration-
That is a position that we support. It comes as a great surprise to realize that the Minister has departed from this decision, and has come to some kind of understanding in Washington about which we have to guess because of the secrecy that surrounds that particular understanding, the plan about which we read in The Globe and Mail, the Toronto Star and other newspapers. There is secrecy, therefore, about the proposal of the EPA to Canada last October. There is secrecy about the understanding that was reached in Washington a day or so ago. There is secrecy within that understanding about the substances that would be removed, reduced and cut, by a percentage that is speculated upon, and by a date that is also speculated upon.
In addition, there is a strange notion on the part of the Minister of the Environment, as revealed this morning, whereby he seems to believe that the United States Government is doing Canada a favour by acceding to our requests and by looking at our proposals. What this Government and the Minister do not seem to realize is that there is an agreement and the United States Government is bound by that agreement, as we are, for the recovery and the quality that has to be improved, hence the name the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, in Lake Ontario and other lakes.
Therefore, there is an international understanding and an agreement signed by the heads of two nations which binds the Americans to look at the Niagara River with the same seriousness as we do. There is no room for interpreting this as a particular favour or nicety. There is a commitment. I hope this will get through the thick skull of the Minister of the Environment once and for all because he does not seem to understand. That is a very serious conceptual flaw in his approach to his American counterpart in dealing with this particular matter. He does not speak up for the Canadian interest with the determination and authority which this agreement gives to him.
I could not believe my eyes when I read in the newspaper about the difference of opinion between the Minister of the Environment in Ottawa and his counterpart in Ontario. The fact that the disagreement was made public is an indication of a poor negotiator, making public a disagreement on the eve of a meeting with the other side. It is also an indication of a poor player who does not understand the importance of having the
Adjournment Debate
full support of all the Canadian Ministers of the Environment on the eve of meeting with his counterpart in Washington.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-NIAGARA RIVER-TOXIC CHEMICAL DUMPS SITES. (B) REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), as usual, has some very firm points with respect to some of the issues which surround the agreement which has been reached by the Canadian Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and the head of the EPA in the United States, Mr. Lee Thomas. Having been able to participate in some of the discussions and deliberations, I have a full sense of the format and conditions under which those agreements were approached. We are now in a position, for the first time since the Love Canal became a national issue, where we in fact have made real solid progress. It is progress which the four million Canadians who drink water from the Niagara region can count on to achieve some results. We could have sat and talked, as former Governments have, for a long time and achieved very little.
Although some of his points have some validity, one of the critical flaws in the approach of the Hon. Member for Davenport to this whole problem is his lack of understanding and appreciation of the information which is available to anyone, and which we must have in order to get the type of firm, hard, clear figures which all of us want inevitably. What I can say is that we have a firm date of July 1, 1987, when we have a commitment with the United States to arrive at those clear-cut targets and loading.
That information is not available to the Province of Ontario, to the American Government nor to the Canadian Government as of today. We have an objective which Mr. Lee Thomas, on behalf of the United States, and the Minister of the Environment of Canada have undertaken together, and perhaps we can exceed the objective of 50 per cent reduction by 1995. That is a major objective on the part of both Governments.
The Hon. Member for Davenport has mentioned the visit by way of the comments made by the Minister of the Environment in Canada insofar as the actions of the Province of Ontario are concerned. Having participated in the meetings with Mr. Thomas, it is unfortunate but there is no question that both Canada and the United States, wanting to co-operate with all parties, have some major concerns regarding the willingness of the Province of Ontario to do anything other than make headlines for its Minister of the Environment.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED ALLEGATIONS MADE BY SUPERINTENDENT. (B) REQUEST FOR INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1973 a joint operation of three police forces, the Montreal Police Force, the Quebec Provincial Police Force and the Royal

May 15, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Canadian Mounted Police, resulted in a break-in at a small news agency in Montreal, VAgence de Presse libre du Quebec.
Five years later the Solicitor General of Canada, Francis Fox, assured the House that this break-in, this breach of the law, was an exceptional and isolated incident and that the directives of the RCMP to its members clearly require that all their actions take place within the law. The statement of the then Solicitor General, Francis Fox, was clearly and utterly without foundation. As the McDonald Commission Report documented, there had been a whole series of breaches of the criminal law by the RCMP prior to 1977.
In late October of last year, a very senior and respected member of the RCMP, Superintendent Nowlan, indicated that the present Commissioner of the RCMP, Commissioner Simmonds, who was the Commissioner Designate in April of 1977, misled the Government of the day and, in particular, misled the Solicitor General with respect to the extent of criminal wrongdoing by the RCMP.
Superintendent Nowlan's allegations are very serious. In many ways they are unprecedented. What he suggested in his allegations was that some 17 days before the Minister made his statement in the House of Commons he, Mr. Nowlan, was ordered to begin an internal inquiry into allegations that . members of the RCMP were involved in illegal operations other than the break-in at the VAgence de Presse libre du Quebec. Those allegations included barn-burning, including involvement of the force in the theft of dynamite, and the use of heavy-handed and illegal tactics to recruit informants in the FLQ.
According to Mr. Nowlan, at least three officers were well aware of the fact that the APLQ incident was not simply an isolated one. Those officers included the then Commissioner Maurice Nadon, the Director of the Security Service Michael Dare, as well as the Commissioner Designate, the current Commissioner Simmonds. Superintendent Nowlan suggested that Simmonds knowingly allowed the Minister to be misled and that because he was not asked the proper questions by the McDonald Commission, the McDonald Commission, as well, allowed the Commissioner Designate to get off the hook with respect to this very serious matter in April of 1977.
On October 31 I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) to conduct an inquiry into these very serious allegations by Superintendent Nowlan. I note that my own Leader, based on the information that he had at the time, suggested that Superintendent Nowlan was responsible for misleading Fox. It is very clear now that that allegation was not well founded. In fact, Superintendent Nowlan was sticking out his neck to make sure that the Solicitor General was well aware of exactly what was going on and it was others, perhaps including the current Commissioner, who chose to deliberately deny access to that important information.
I asked the Solicitor General what action he intended to take with respect to these very serious allegations. The Solicitor General said that he intended to take no action whatsoever. Why was this? Because he had spoken with Francis Fox and Francis Fox said that he was not aware of being misled.
One must ask who in fact is in charge. Surely the Solicitor General had an obligation to meet with Commissioner Simmonds and put these allegations to him directly. How would Francis Fox know if he had not been given the information in question? Instead, the Solicitor General refused to conduct an investigation.
I have sought to have the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee give Superintendent Nowlan an opportunity to appear before it to present evidence. I suggest that the call of the former Superintendent who retired recently for an independent inquiry with the power to examine documents at National Headquarters is one which I fully support. Yet it has been stonewalled and denied by the Minister.
Who in fact is in charge? We have heard the rather contemptible suggestions made by the Commissioner that Superintendent Nowlan had certain mental problems, so his allegations should be discredited. While it is quite accurate to suggest that Superintendent Nowlan does suffer from manic depression, his doctor has made it very clear that he is a man of integrity and sound judgment. In addition, the former Solicitor General, Francis Fox, spoke very highly indeed of Superintendent Nowlan and called him a very honourable and a very thorough person.
In view of the seriousness of these allegations and in view of the fact that Superintendent Nowlan was well aware of what was going on and the extent of knowledge within the RCMP, particularly at the senior levels, 1 call upon the Minister once again to allow this matter to be examined. After all, what does he have to hide? Allow the Justice Committee to invite Superintendent Nowlan to appear before it. Appoint an independent investigator to get to the bottom of these very serious allegations.
I suggest that Superintendent Nowlan should be commended by Canadians and by the House for having the courage to speak out before he retired with respect to these matters. I would hope that instead of continuing to cover up these allegations which after all affect the Commissioner himself and his position, they should be fully investigated.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED ALLEGATIONS MADE BY SUPERINTENDENT. (B) REQUEST FOR INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has raised newspaper accounts of allegations made by an officer of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police concerning the conduct of senior officers of the force. These allegations related to matters which were the subject of deliberations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry established
May 15, 1986

in 1977 under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice David McDonald and assisted by D. S. Rickard, Q.C., and Guy Gilbert, Q.C.
The key components of the mandate of this commission were to conduct such investigations as were necessary to determine the extent and prevalence of investigative practices involving members of the RCMP that were not authorized or provided for by law and to report the facts and to advise as to any action deemed necessary in the public interest about such matters.
Hon. Members will recall that in discharging its responsibilities, this Commission operated from July 1977 until August 1981, four years and 50 days. During that time, Mr. Justice McDonald and his colleagues searched for and heard testimony about these matters at a level of intensity and detail unprecedented in respect to the activities of the RCMP, its personnel or this general sector of Government operations.
The facts are clear. There were hearings of two kinds, evidentiary and those requiring briefs. Evidentiary hearings were held both in public and in camera. One hundred and sixty-nine public hearings and 144 in camera hearings were held at which 149 witnesses were examined and 105 exhibits received. Superintendent Nowlan was one of those witnesses. Public briefs were heard twice in Vancouver and some five times in Regina, Toronto, Montreal, Fredericton, and Ottawa. There were several volumes of public reports, and to supplement hearing information, the commission met informally with many groups and individuals.
What then of the allegations about the conduct of the present Commissioner of the RCMP, Robert Simmonds, relating to the matters examined by the royal commission? I refer Hon. Members to the second report, Volume I entitled "Freedom and Security Under the Law", where at page 7, paragraph 23, the Commissioners concluded the following:
Robert Simmonds became Commissioner of the RCMP on September 1, 1977, almost at the same time as this Commission was established. Before that, since 1976, he had been the Deputy Commissioner responsible for administration, and his brief time in that position was his only prior experience at headquarters; all his earlier career, from the time he joined the RCMP in 1947, was spent in Alberta and British Columbia. Managing a police force the size of the RCMP is a difficult task at the best times. Commissioner Simmonds' burden has been increased greatly during the past three and one-half years by the activities of our inquiry and those of the provincial inquiries. His stance vis-a-vis this Commission has been, throughout, one of total co-operation. We are conscious of the fact that he has put on hold certain plans and proposals that he had for change within the Force, pending receipt of our report, and also that he has felt constrained to suspend or terminate certain practices merely because to continue them might have meant to continue unlawful conduct. Our inquiry and report touched only occasionally upon Commissioner Simmonds. He inherited the situation which led to our inquiry and participated in neither the formulation nor the continuation of the policies which have been its substance.
This royal commission had unrestricted access to every RCMP and almost every other Government record it wished to examine, and to any RCMP officer and other Government official it wished to question including the then Prime Minister. It was in full possession of the facts and thus in the only position to draw the appropriate conclusions. In this context,
Adjournment Debate
these allegations directed at Commissioner Simmonds seem particularly ill-advised, to say the least. This point brings me to the last observation which I wish to make on this issue.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is justifiably a well-respected institution in Canada. I say justifiably because of the way it links us to our past, because of the unparalleled record of service its personnel has provided to Canadians, and because of the universality of the regard and recognition it affords for Canada abroad. These are the facts, no less conclusive than the commission of inquiry's estimation of Mr. Simmonds.
In conclusion, I wish to state the Government's view that the facts as reported by the McDonald Commission speak for themselves, and that the call for another inquiry into these allegations is totally unjustifiable.
AGRICULTURE-EFFECT OF REDUCED INITIAL PRICE, (fi) REQUEST FOR 1985 INITIAL PRICE

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED ALLEGATIONS MADE BY SUPERINTENDENT. (B) REQUEST FOR INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 10, I directed a question to the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). I asked him how he expected farmers in western Canada to survive when just a day or two before he announced the lowest initial prices for wheat, barley, and other grains in real dollars since the 1930s. The Minister's response to that request was essentially to slough off the question. He ended his response by saying:
The problem we face is a larger problem, that is, very depressed world grain prices.
Was that a brilliant response to a serious question about how Canadians would survive?
The fact of the matter is that Canadian grain producers will be receiving about $1.50 per bushel for No. 1 wheat. Of course we have to take into account the cost of handling and transportation. The net return will be something over $3 Canadian, whereas United States farmers in the mid-West will be receiving over $6 Canadian per bushel this year regardless of the world price. For example, if the world price is $3.50 or $2.50 per bushel, they will still receive $6 plus per bushel.
Again I ask the Minister how he expects farmers in western Canada to survive when they are receiving about half as much per bushel of wheat as their American counterparts.
The doom and gloom hanging over western Canada is unprecedented, I believe, since the 1930s because the United States and the European Economic Community are engaged in an agricultural commodity price war. The United States Congress has voted sufficient funds to fight the war for the next three years. Its law provides funds for five years. The visits of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to Washington produced no results, assistance or backing off by the United States Government on the impact of that stablization, subsidization and bonus program.
When the Prime Minister went to the Economic Summit in Japan, he said he was going to raise the matter. I believe he

May 15, 1986
Adjournment Debate
did. There was no indication in the communique from the conference that the seven heads of Government would take any action with regard to the grain and agricultural commodity price war. The communique indicated that they would not even refer the matter of agricultural commodities to the negotiating table at the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade talks. That is a disaster for Canadian farmers. Everyone will have to hunker down to the prospect of a trade war. If the seven nations do not press to have agricultural commodities on the negotiating agenda in the GATT conference in Uraguay this fall, it means the agricultural commodity price war between the European Economic Community and the United States will go on. Not to have it on the agenda is a tremendous failure on the part of the Prime Minister.
I appreciate the fact that he raised the matter, met with farmers and their representatives in Vancouver, but the farmers are left defenceless. The Prime Minister and the Government must announce immediately a deficiency payment program to stabilize and secure the western economy. At the moment the western economy, especially in Alberta and Saskatchewan, is reeling from the impact of low oil prices. Not to provide minimum support for the grain industry will be devastating.
When the Parliamentary Secretary speaks tonight, it is essential that he immediately announce at the bare minimum financial assistance which the three prairie pools, the Western Grain Growers Association and other western farm organizations have asked for. They need a stabilization deficiency payment adequate to secure and maintain that industry during the coming crop year and in years ahead. One approach might be to reinstate the 1985 grain prices which would tell the farmers that the Government was not prepared to provide as much financial assistance as the United States Government does, but that there would be some financial assistance to stabilize and secure the whole western economy during the coming year.
If action is not taken now by the federal Government, there will be a serious financial crisis on the Prairies. There will be bankruptcies and farm losses. There will be a loss of the entire rural economy. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will come forward and make that commitment tonight so that western agricultural and grain producers will know where they stand. They will know what their future is going to be and that the Government is going to support and assist them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED ALLEGATIONS MADE BY SUPERINTENDENT. (B) REQUEST FOR INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always a little bit surprised when I hear my colleague the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) echo day in and day out the same fears and concerns expressed over the past 18 months by members of his Party about the farm industry. Given his considerable experience, he is well aware that Canadian grain producers are caught in a cross-fire of sort, in the war that is being waged between the European Economic Community and the United States.
Canada is the innocent victim of the large scale war which two of the world economic powers are waging through massive subsidies to their respective agricultural industries.
We have tried to ease the burden of grain producers by reducing to 19 per cent the cut in initial prices which could have been a lot worse and which is a lot less than that made in the American prices.
When initial prices were announced, it was also announced that tariffs administered by the Canadian Grain Commission have been frozen at last year's levels. These include cleaning, elevation and storage charges at terminal and county elevators. The Government is acting in other ways. It is studying domestic wheat prices. A special parliamentary committee chaired by the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) is studying ways of increasing returns to wheat producers. The committee is expected to report to Parliament in mid-June.
When Members opposite call on the Government to do more for prairie farmers, they seem to have lost sight of the fact that the Government has done a lot for farmers already. It has announced policies and programs which have resulted in $4 billion in benefits to farmers, of which $1.5 billion has been channelled to western farmers in particular.

The Hon. Member should not disregard this fact nor ignore the efforts which our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made. He has described this as a defeat. Is it possible to speak of a defeat when for the first time a Prime Minister, at an international meeting of seven world powers, has managed to have it appear on the agenda and convince these powers that it is absolutely necessary to do something to end this price war? On the eve of his departure for Tokyo, the Prime Minister had met all the Canadians representatives of the farm industry to seek their advice before meeting the representatives of the seven major powers.
Something else that had never been done in the past, Mr. Speaker, is that our Minister, the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) is going to meet with representatives of other wheat exporting nations in Vancouver in a few weeks from now.
I therefore feel, Mr. Speaker, that this Government has made every effort, everything it could in the current farmers' crisis of which we are well aware, to make sure Canadian producers are well represented and get the best deal in the circumstances.
